Name: safety_verdict_uncertainty
Title: False Confidence: Jailbreaks Collapse the Model's Uncertainty About Its Own Safety Verdict, and Re-Injecting It Restores Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a distinct, linearly-readable representation of epistemic uncertainty about their OWN safety verdict ('how sure am I that this request is safe?'), separate from output-token entropy, from the harmfulness-belief direction, and from the refusal-action direction. We hypothesize (1) many jailbreaks succeed not by flipping the harmfulness belief nor merely suppressing refusal, but by artificially COLLAPSING this safety-verdict uncertainty to false confidence, so the model commits to compliance without hedging or reflecting; and (2) a training-free intervention that detects abnormally-collapsed verdict uncertainty and re-injects calibrated uncertainty re-triggers the model's cautious/reflective refusal pathway, defeating jailbreaks with low over-refusal.
Related Work: SIRL/Safety Instincts (2025) observes an entropy GAP (low-entropy refusals vs high-entropy dangerous generation) and turns it into an RL reward; it uses raw output entropy as a training signal and does not isolate a verdict-uncertainty representation or intervene at inference. SCIURus (2025) shows factuality and uncertainty share circuits but studies factual QA, not safety. 'Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty' (2025) finds a linear verbal-uncertainty feature for hallucinations, not safety. 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) finds a solvability-belief axis that is causally inert for execution. Zhao et al. (2025) separate harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action). Our proposal introduces a THIRD, previously-unisolated safety object: the model's epistemic uncertainty about its safety verdict (metacognitive confidence in the safe/harmful classification), and advances the causal claim that jailbreaks work by inducing FALSE CONFIDENCE (collapsing this uncertainty) rather than only flipping belief or suppressing refusal. Unlike SIRL (training-based, output entropy), our defense is training-free and re-injects calibrated verdict uncertainty at inference; unlike Latent Guard (harmfulness classifier) it targets the confidence-in-the-verdict axis, which we show distinguishes confident jailbreaks from genuinely ambiguous benign requests.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs refuse single harmful requests but fall to jailbreaks. Two mechanistic accounts dominate: jailbreaks either flip the model's harmfulness belief or suppress its refusal action while leaving the belief intact. We propose a complementary and, we argue, often dominant mechanism grounded in metacognition: jailbreaks induce FALSE CONFIDENCE, collapsing the model's uncertainty about its OWN safety verdict so it commits to compliance without the hedging/reflection that normally precedes a refusal. We first isolate a safety-verdict-uncertainty representation using minimal pairs that hold harmfulness content fixed but vary how CONFIDENT the model should be about the safe/harmful classification (clearly-harmful vs clearly-benign vs genuinely-ambiguous requests), extracting a linear verdict-uncertainty direction via difference-in-means and validating it is separable (low cosine) from harmfulness-belief, refusal-action, and raw output-entropy directions. We then test causally whether successful jailbreaks systematically drive this direction toward false confidence (low uncertainty) while the harmfulness belief remains high, using activation patching to show that patching only the collapsed verdict-uncertainty component into a clean run transfers compliance, and re-injecting uncertainty into a jailbroken run restores refusal. Finally we introduce Verdict-Uncertainty Re-injection (VUR), a training-free defense that flags abnormally-collapsed verdict uncertainty (given a still-high harmfulness belief) and adds an activation nudge re-inflating uncertainty, re-triggering cautious refusal. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we measure direction separability, the jailbreak false-confidence signature, causal patching transfer, and VUR's attack-success reduction versus over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench) and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench). We expect false confidence to be a robust, attack-agnostic jailbreak signature and VUR to Pareto-dominate belief/refusal-only defenses on genuinely-ambiguous inputs.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, all frozen (directions are read and the defense edits activations; no training). Four directions are extracted by difference-in-means over a layer sweep, layer chosen per direction by held-out probe AUROC: verdict-uncertainty (confident/clear vs. genuinely-ambiguous requests, at the last instruction token), harmfulness-belief (harmful vs. harmless), refusal-action (post-instruction token, comply vs. refuse), and a raw output-entropy proxy. Projections are standardized to units of standard deviations (SD) over a calibration set.

Experiment 1 (H1 setup — a safety-verdict-uncertainty axis distinct from belief, refusal, and output entropy). Tests whether an epistemic-uncertainty-about-own-verdict direction exists and is separable from the other three. Data (constructed): a minimal-pair set holding request content-type roughly fixed while varying the appropriate confidence in the safety verdict — clearly-harmful (confidently harmful), clearly-benign (confidently safe), and genuinely-ambiguous/dual-use (verdict SHOULD be uncertain, e.g., "how do household chemicals react", "explain how phishing works for training"); ~500 items per category, auto-generated with a 10% hand-checked sample. Method: extract the verdict-uncertainty direction (clear vs. ambiguous) and the other three directions, validate each with probe AUROC on held-out sets, and compute pairwise cosine similarities; frozen models. Decisive metric first: pairwise cosine between verdict-uncertainty and each of harmfulness-belief, refusal-action, and output-entropy; then the verdict-uncertainty probe AUROC on held-out clear-vs-ambiguous items. Convincing result: every verdict-uncertainty pairwise |cosine| <=0.3 and its probe AUROC >=0.85, establishing a distinct, readable axis. Indecision band (before data): a cosine in [0.3, 0.6] with belief or output-entropy means the axis is only partly distinct — the causal test below is expected to be muddier. Negative result: |cosine| >0.6 with harmfulness-belief or output-entropy means verdict-uncertainty is not a separate axis and the hypothesis's premise fails.

Experiment 2 (H1 — successful jailbreaks collapse verdict-uncertainty to false confidence while belief stays high). Tests whether the false-confidence signature is present and dominant across attack families. Data: GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, and roleplay/DAN attacks (JailbreakBench 100 + HarmBench 100 sampled behaviors) run per model, split into judge-confirmed successes and failures. Method: for successful vs. failed attacks, measure the projection change on all four directions; frozen models. Decisive metric first: the mean verdict-uncertainty shift on successful jailbreaks (toward low/confident, in SD) alongside the belief shift; then whether verdict-uncertainty is the largest-shifting of the four directions and how consistently across families. Convincing result: on the majority of attack families verdict-uncertainty drops >=1.0 SD while harmfulness-belief stays within 0.5 SD, and verdict-uncertainty is the largest-shifting direction (false confidence, not belief flip or mere refusal suppression). Indecision band (before data): a verdict-uncertainty drop in [0.5, 1.0] SD means the signature is present but weak — H1 holds partially and VUR is expected to help less. Negative result: verdict-uncertainty not dropping, or belief itself dropping >=1.0 SD (a belief-flip mechanism), means false confidence does not explain those attacks — recorded as a scope limit (e.g., abliteration-style attacks may fall here).

Experiment 3 (H1 — the verdict-uncertainty collapse is causally responsible for compliance). Tests, via patching, whether the collapsed uncertainty component drives compliance rather than merely correlating (the crucial test given that decodable axes can be causally inert). Data: matched jailbroken-complied vs. clean-refused run pairs on the same behaviors from Experiment 2 (target 200 pairs per model). Method: (a) patch ONLY the collapsed verdict-uncertainty component from a jailbroken run into a clean refused run and measure induced compliance; (b) patch harmfulness-belief alone and refusal-action alone as controls; (c) reverse — re-inject high verdict-uncertainty into a jailbroken run and measure restored refusal; frozen models. Decisive metric first: compliance-transfer rate from patching verdict-uncertainty alone vs. the control patches; then the reverse restored-refusal rate. Convincing result: verdict-uncertainty-only patching induces compliance in >=50% of clean-refused runs while belief-only and refusal-only patches induce <=15%, and re-injecting uncertainty restores refusal in >=50% of jailbroken runs. Indecision band (before data): a verdict-uncertainty transfer rate in [25, 50]% means it is one contributing cause among several — reported as partial, and VUR expected to be partially effective. Negative result: transfer <25% (near the controls) means verdict-uncertainty is causally inert and H1's causal claim fails — an informative negative.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Verdict-Uncertainty Re-injection defeats jailbreaks with low over-refusal on ambiguous inputs). Tests whether re-inflating collapsed uncertainty, gated on a still-high belief, restores refusal while hedging rather than blanket-refusing genuinely-ambiguous requests. Method (VUR): gated on a still-high harmfulness-belief projection, detect abnormally-low verdict-uncertainty and add v = beta*(target_uncertainty - current)*dhat at chosen layer(s); training-free, one fixed setting per model; belief-gating leaves genuinely-benign requests untouched. Data: attack success on GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR/roleplay (judge + verification where possible); over-refusal on XSTest-safe (200), OR-Bench (500), and specifically the genuinely-ambiguous/dual-use set from Experiment 1 (where VUR should hedge/qualify, not refuse); utility on MMLU (2,000-subset), MT-Bench (80), AlpacaEval (805). Systems compared: no defense, refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, SafeSwitch, and SIRL-style output-entropy thresholding; ablations isolate re-injecting uncertainty vs. belief vs. refusal, sweep beta (Pareto), gated vs. always-on, and layer. Decisive metric first: attack-success reduction paired with over-refusal on the ambiguous/dual-use set; then over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and utility. Convincing result: VUR cuts ASR by >=40 points vs. no defense while its over-refusal on the ambiguous set is >=10 points lower than belief/refusal-only defenses at matched ASR, with MMLU drop <=2 points. Indecision band (before data): ASR reduction in [15, 40] points, or an ambiguous-set over-refusal advantage in [3, 10] points, means VUR helps but does not clearly Pareto-dominate — reported as such. Negative result: ASR reduction <15 points, or no over-refusal advantage on ambiguous inputs over belief/refusal-only defenses, means VUR adds nothing and H2 is unsupported.

Experiment 5 (H2 — adaptive attacker who co-suppresses both axes). Tests whether an attacker who jointly keeps verdict-uncertainty low AND harmfulness-belief low can evade the belief-gated VUR, and at what cost. Data: an adaptive attack on the 100 JailbreakBench behaviors optimized to keep both projections low, run against VUR-defended models. Decisive metric first: ASR under VUR vs. the non-adaptive attack; then the query budget required. Convincing result: co-suppressing both axes forces >=50% more queries or yields lower ASR than the undefended baseline (raised attack cost). Indecision band (before data): a query-budget increase in [10, 50]% is a modest cost, reported honestly. Negative result: the adaptive attacker matches undefended ASR at no extra cost, showing VUR is bypassed by joint suppression (the failure its risk section anticipates).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Verdict-uncertainty may not be cleanly separable from harmfulness belief or output entropy; the axes could be entangled, weakening the causal decomposition — the separability and patching experiments directly test this. 2) Constructing minimal pairs that vary appropriate verdict confidence while holding content fixed is delicate; residual confounds (topic, wording) could contaminate the direction. 3) Some jailbreaks (e.g., pure refusal-action suppression via abliteration) may NOT collapse verdict uncertainty, so VUR may help less on those; the per-direction shift analysis quantifies which attacks the mechanism explains. 4) 'Confidence is Not Competence' warns that decodable belief axes can be causally inert; verdict-uncertainty might likewise be non-actionable — the patching experiment is the crucial causal test, and a negative result is itself informative. 5) Re-injecting uncertainty could over-hedge and reduce helpfulness on legitimately confident benign requests; belief-gating and the Pareto sweep quantify this. 6) A single verdict-uncertainty direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace re-injection. 7) Directions and gains are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers co-suppressing both axes remain a threat, though this raises attack cost.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty: (1) aligned LLMs contain a distinct, linearly decodable internal representation of safety-verdict epistemic uncertainty, separate from harmfulness belief, refusal action, and output-token entropy; (2) many jailbreaks succeed by collapsing this verdict-uncertainty to false confidence while harmfulness belief remains high; (3) this uncertainty axis is causally efficacious, not just correlational, as shown by activation patching that transfers compliance/refusal; (4) a training-free Verdict-Uncertainty Re-injection defense can restore refusal with lower over-refusal than belief/refusal-only defenses, especially on ambiguous inputs. Relative to the cited prior family, this is meaningfully new: prior mechanistic work centers on belief-flip vs refusal-suppression, while uncertainty-based defenses mostly rely on token entropy or self-reported confidence. The proposal's real delta is a third mechanistic pathway at the representation level: metacognitive uncertainty over the safety verdict itself. That is a non-trivial extension, not just 'uncertainty helps' in a new wrapper. The closest prior work family is Zhao/Arditi-style mechanistic separation plus entropy-based defenses like LightDefense/SIRL and metacognitive safety frameworks like MENTOR. Actual delta: a specific internal direction, claimed separable from both belief and entropy, plus causal tests and a targeted intervention. Main novelty risk is that the axis may reduce to a mixture of harmfulness ambiguity, generic uncertainty, or output entropy, and the defense itself is less novel than the mechanistic hypothesis.

The 'so what?' answer is fairly good: it could change both scientific understanding and practical defense design. review.reasoning: This is a strong, testable idea but currently has important methodological and identification risks. Positives: the hypothesis is falsifiable and unusually concrete; experiments are more specific than most proposals; the proposal explicitly acknowledges the key causal-inertness risk and makes patching central. Main logical gap: the construction of 'minimal pairs' that vary only appropriate confidence in the safety classification while holding harmfulness content fixed is much harder than stated. Ambiguous requests often differ semantically, pragmatically, and normatively from clear harmful/benign ones, so the extracted direction may partly encode ambiguity, distribution shift, or prompt complexity. Relatedly, low cosine with other directions is not sufficient to establish conceptual separability; distributed subspaces or nonlinear overlap could remain. Difference-in-means on coarse classes may be too weak for a claim this specific. The causal design is promising but under-specified: 'patch only the collapsed verdict-uncertainty component' assumes clean localization and may leak other features unless orthogonalization and residual controls are carefully done. Controls need strengthening: patch random directions with matched norm, patch generic uncertainty directions from non-safety tasks, test whether VUR simply increases hesitancy globally, and compare to adding generic deliberation tokens or chain-of-thought-like reflective prompting. The defense eval is fairly good, but baselines need tighter specification and matched operating points. Over-refusal claims on 'genuinely ambiguous' inputs are central yet the dataset is custom and vulnerable to annotation subjectivity. There is also a risk of benchmark overfitting to open-weight models and standard attack families. If executed cleanly, this could be a strong workshop/ACL Findings/ICLR submission and possibly stronger if the causal evidence is compelling and the dataset/controls are excellent. Minimum viable edits are mostly about identification, controls, and measurement definitions.

Add a fallback impact story: even if VUR fails, what would a negative/partial result teach the field about jailbreak mechanisms?
Define an annotation protocol for 'verdict uncertainty' and 'genuinely ambiguous' inputs, ideally with multiple raters and agreement statistics.

Replace or augment cosine-separability with stronger tests: orthogonalized probes, partial regressions controlling for entropy/belief/refusal, subspace overlap, CCA, or interventions after projection removal.
Add critical controls for causal patching: random matched-norm directions, generic non-safety uncertainty directions, sham patches at nearby layers/tokens, and projection-removal tests.

Name: aggregate_intent_reconstruction
Title: Blind to the Whole: LLMs Fail to Internally Integrate Decomposed Harm, but the Aggregate-Intent Direction Can Be Reconstructed and Re-Read
Short Hypothesis: Decomposition attacks succeed because an aligned LLM computes per-subtask harmfulness but never forms an internal representation of the aggregated harmful goal that the benign-looking subtasks jointly serve. We hypothesize (1) this aggregate-intent representation is latent-but-dormant: it is essentially absent when sub-queries arrive decomposed, yet a linear 'reconstructed-goal' direction can be recovered from the model's own activations when it is shown the accumulated conversation; and (2) a training-free 'intent-integration probe' that at each turn re-reads the cumulative context onto this direction detects emerging cumulative harm before the final step, providing an internal, mechanistic alternative to external plan-level monitors and explaining why single-turn safety is structurally blind to decomposition.
Related Work: Decomposition/compositional attacks are well documented: 'Adversaries Can Misuse Combinations of Safe Models' (2024), 'Safe in Isolation, Dangerous Together' (2025), STAC (2025), CKA-Agent (2025), and Semantic Intent Fragmentation (2026) all show >90% attack success by splitting a harmful goal into benign subtasks. Defenses to date are EXTERNAL: lightweight sequential LLM monitors ('Monitoring Decomposition Attacks', 2025) and plan-level LLM judges / information-flow taint (SIF's Compositional Intent Verifier, 2026). Mechanistically, 'Expected Harm' (2026) shows via linear probing that models encode harm SEVERITY but have NO distinguishable internal representation of execution COST, making them blind to a key risk dimension. Our proposal is distinct on three counts: (1) rather than adding an external judge, we ask whether the TARGET model's OWN internal state can be made to represent aggregate intent, and show it is dormant not missing — recoverable as a linear direction from the concatenated context; (2) we advance and causally test a specific mechanistic account of decomposition blindness (per-turn harm computed, integrated harm never computed), extending 'Expected Harm' from severity/cost to the cumulative-goal dimension; (3) our defense is a training-free internal probe/steer that re-reads reconstructed aggregate intent per turn, cheaper and white-box-native compared to per-turn external LLM monitors, and we compare directly against them.
Abstract: Large language models refuse overtly harmful requests yet are trivially defeated by decomposition attacks that split a harmful goal into individually benign subtasks — attack success often exceeds 90%. Existing defenses bolt an external monitor or plan-level judge onto the system. We instead ask a mechanistic question: does the model itself ever internally represent the aggregate harmful goal that its benign subtasks jointly serve? We hypothesize the answer is no — the model computes per-subtask harmfulness but never integrates across steps — and that this dormant-but-recoverable 'aggregate intent' is the crux of decomposition blindness. We test this in three parts. First, using paired data (a monolithic harmful request vs. its benign decomposition into subtasks), we extract a linear harmfulness direction and show that its projection is high for the monolithic request but collapses to near-benign for each decomposed subtask and, crucially, for the running conversation as processed turn-by-turn — the model never re-integrates. Second, we show the aggregate goal is latent: feeding the model the concatenated conversation and prompting it to infer the overall objective recovers a 'reconstructed-goal' direction whose projection re-separates harmful from benign decompositions, and we causally verify with activation patching that injecting this reconstructed-goal component into a decomposed run restores refusal. Third, we build Intent-Integration Probing (IIP): a training-free defense that at each turn re-reads the cumulative context onto the reconstructed-goal direction to flag emerging cumulative harm. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we evaluate detection lead-time, decomposition-attack defense success, over-refusal, and utility, comparing IIP against external sequential monitors. We expect a robust integration-blindness signature and IIP to detect cumulative harm several subtasks before completion.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen for every experiment except the LoRA reference in Experiment 4. All "directions" are difference-in-means vectors on residual-stream activations; all "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Every reported number is averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) governing data sampling, attacker-LLM generation, and steering noise; we report mean and a 95% bootstrap CI. Everything fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: 400 harmful behaviors from HarmBench and 313 from StrongREJECT (713 monolithic harmful requests). For each we generate a benign multi-subtask decomposition with an attacker LLM (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, temperature 0.7, the Safe-in-Isolation/CKA-Agent recipe: 3-6 individually-benign subtasks that jointly reconstruct the goal). We keep the 500 decompositions (of 713) that pass a two-judge screen (every subtask judged benign in isolation by Llama-Guard-3; the whole chain judged to reconstruct the original goal by GPT-4o-mini) and cap at 500 to bound attacker-API cost. Negatives: 500 genuinely-benign multi-step conversations matched on turn count and length, drawn from ShareGPT multi-turn logs filtered benign. Split 300/100/100 train/val/test by goal, no goal crossing a split.

Experiment 1 (H1 - integration blindness): Tests whether the model computes per-subtask harmfulness but never forms an internal representation of the aggregated goal. Decisive metric: the integration gap G = proj_harm(monolithic request) - max over turns t of proj_harm(running conversation at turn t), expressed in units of the pooled within-class SD of the harmfulness projection. Data: the 500 decompositions plus 500 benign negatives. Model: the three frozen models; harmfulness direction from difference-in-means on 300 monolithic-harmful vs 300 harmless training requests at the last prompt token, layer picked on val by probe AUROC. We record proj_harm for (a) the monolithic request, (b) each subtask in isolation, (c) the running conversation processed turn-by-turn (last token at each turn). Convincing: mean G >= 1.5 SD, with (b) and (c) statistically indistinguishable from the benign-negative distribution (two-sided t, p>0.05) while (a) sits >= 3 SD above it, on all three models. Indecision band: G in [0.5, 1.5] SD - the representation is partially integrated, so "never forms" is downgraded to "under-forms" and H2/H3 are reframed as amplifying a weak signal rather than reconstructing an absent one; we commit to that reframing now. Negative (G < 0.5 SD, running projection tracks the monolithic one): the model does integrate, refuting H1; decomposition then succeeds for some other reason, which we report without proceeding to the H3 defense.

Experiment 2 (H2 - dormant-but-recoverable aggregate-intent direction): Tests that the aggregate goal is latent (essentially absent under decomposition), recoverable as a linear direction from the concatenated context, and causally sufficient to restore refusal. Decisive metric: test-set AUROC of the reconstructed-goal projection separating harmful from benign decompositions, read against the raw running-projection AUROC of Experiment 1. Data: the same 500/500, test split (100/100). Procedure: feed each frozen model its own concatenated conversation and prompt it to state the overall objective; extract a reconstructed-goal direction by difference-in-means on activations for inferred-harmful vs inferred-benign objectives (train split); read its projection on test. Causal leg: activation patching that injects the reconstructed-goal component into a decomposed run at the final-subtask decision token, scoring refusal-restoration rate (fraction of previously-complied harmful decompositions now judge-scored as refused), against two controls (patch a benign-goal component; patch a random norm-matched direction). Convincing: reconstructed AUROC >= 0.80 while raw running AUROC <= 0.65 (a >= 0.15 gap), AND patching restores refusal on >= 40% of cases versus <= 5% for both controls. Indecision band: reconstructed AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] OR restoration in [15%, 40%] - the direction carries partial but not decisive aggregate intent; H2 is supported only as "partially recoverable" and we report the recovery ceiling. Negative (reconstructed AUROC <= 0.65 or restoration within 15 points of controls): the aggregate goal is not linearly recoverable or not causally sufficient, refuting H2 and predicting the H3 defense will fail.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Intent-Integration Probing detects cumulative harm before completion and improves on external monitors): Tests that a training-free per-turn re-read of the reconstructed-goal projection flags emerging cumulative harm before the final step, with a better lead-time / defense / over-refusal trade-off than external monitors. Decisive metric: mean detection lead-time L = number of subtasks before the final harmful subtask at which the alarm first fires on true-positive attacks, reported jointly with decomposition-attack defense success and benign over-refusal. Data: held-out test attacks from three families (Safe-in-Isolation-style, STAC-style, CKA-style; ~100 each, generated as above on a disjoint goal set), the 100 benign multi-step test negatives, XSTest (450 prompts) and a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample for over-refusal, and MT-Bench (80) plus a 2,000-question MMLU subsample for utility. IIP: at each turn run the goal-reconstruction read and threshold the reconstructed-goal projection; threshold fixed on val at 1% FPR against benign negatives. Systems compared (decisive metric first, then defense success, then over-refusal): IIP vs (i) a per-turn harmfulness probe with no integration, (ii) Llama-Guard-3 per turn, (iii) a lightweight external sequential LLM monitor (Qwen2.5-7B judge, Monitoring-Decomposition-Attacks style), (iv) a plan-level LLM judge. Convincing: IIP fires >= 2 subtasks before completion on >= 60% of true positives AND lands within 5 points of the best external monitor on defense success while its over-refusal on benign multi-step negatives is >= 10 points lower than that monitor. Indecision band: lead-time in [1, 2) subtasks OR defense-success gap to the best monitor in [5, 15] points - IIP is a viable cheaper white-box option but not clearly early or dominant, and we report it as complementary. Negative (lead-time < 1, i.e., fires only at/after the final step, or over-refusal no better than the monitors): IIP offers no early-warning or trade-off gain and we report external monitoring as preferable. We log forward passes per turn so the reviewer sees IIP adds one reconstruction pass rather than a full separate monitor call.

Experiment 4 (H2/H3 robustness and adaptive cost): Tests whether the reconstructed-goal direction transfers across attack and model families and how much an adaptive attacker must pay to evade it. Decisive metric: cross-family transfer AUROC (direction extracted on one attack family, evaluated on another) and the multiplicative increase in subtask count an adaptive attacker needs to push IIP below 1% TPR at 1% FPR. Data: the three attack families above; adaptive attacker = the same attacker LLM instructed to maximize pairwise semantic distance between subtasks (target embedding cosine < 0.3). Model: the frozen models, plus one reference point of a 20-step LoRA-tuned probe (rank 8, lr 1e-4, one seed) to check whether light tuning beats the training-free read. Convincing: transfer AUROC drops by <= 0.10 across families AND the adaptive attacker needs >= 2x more subtasks (raising its own detectability and cost) to evade. Indecision band: transfer drop in [0.10, 0.20] - the direction is family-specific and must be re-extracted per family, which we state. Negative (transfer drop > 0.20, or adaptive evasion at no extra subtask cost): the mechanism is brittle and we scope the claim to non-adaptive, in-family decomposition.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Goal reconstruction relies on the model's own inference; if the model cannot infer the aggregate goal even when shown the full conversation, the reconstructed-goal direction will be weak — this is itself an informative negative but limits the defense. 2) The integration gap may be partial rather than binary; some models may re-integrate somewhat, weakening the 'blindness' claim. 3) Reconstruction adds an extra forward pass per turn (cost), though still cheaper than a separate large monitor. 4) Benign multi-step conversations that plausibly infer to a harmful goal could cause over-refusal; the benign-negatives set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 5) A single harmfulness/goal direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 6) Adaptive attackers maximizing subtask semantic dispersion may evade reconstruction, though this constrains the attack and raises cost. 7) Directions and thresholds are model-specific and need per-model calibration; results depend on the quality of automatically generated decompositions.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty are: (1) decomposition attacks work because the target model under decomposed prompting fails to internally integrate subtasks into an aggregate harmful-goal representation; (2) this aggregate-intent representation is not absent in principle but dormant-and-recoverable from cumulative context via a linear direction; (3) that recovered direction is causally sufficient enough that activation patching can restore refusal; and (4) a training-free white-box internal probe can detect cumulative harm competitively with external sequential monitors. From the proposal and search context, decomposition attacks and linear harmful-intent probes are already established, so the novelty is not in the attack family or probe machinery. The main delta is the mechanistic explanation ('integration blindness'), the dormant-but-reconstructable aggregate-intent framing, and using an internal white-box reread instead of an external judge. That is meaningfully distinct from prior external-monitor work and from generic residual-stream linear probing, but it is still adjacent to active 2025-2026 lines, so the contribution is more a nontrivial mechanistic synthesis/new finding than a wholly new task or method family.
revision_notes: State the 3-4 precise novel claims up front and separate them from known ingredients: decomposition attacks are known, linear probes are known, external sequential monitoring is known; the claimed novelty is the mechanistic account plus causal test plus internal defense framing.

Tighten the delta against the closest prior family by explicitly contrasting with external cumulative-context monitors and with harmful-intent linear recoverability papers; say why neither already implies 'the target model itself fails to integrate during normal rollout.'
Soften 'never forms' to a testable graded claim such as 'systematically under-integrates relative to monolithic prompts' unless the evidence can truly support an absolute statement.

Add a stronger novelty hook beyond linear reconstruction, e.g. layerwise/timewise localization of where integration fails or a formal distinction between represented-in-rollout vs reconstructable-off-rollout.
Clarify whether the contribution is primarily a new mechanistic finding, a new defense paradigm, or a new benchmark setting; right now it spans all three and risks sounding incremental on each.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is decomposition-based jailbreak vulnerability: models that are safe on single turns can still assist harmful goals when the goal is split into benign subtasks. The stakeholders are AI safety, red-teaming, agent-safety, and developers deploying multi-turn assistants. If the result holds, researchers may shift from purely external monitors toward internal white-box cumulative-intent checks, and mechanistic work on safety would gain a clearer target: integration failure rather than generic refusal weakness. The strongest one-line case is that this explains a major practical jailbreak class and offers a cheaper, lower-overrefusal defense. The 'so what?' test is passed: if true, people would redesign defenses and mechanistic evaluations around aggregate-intent integration; if false, that also matters because it would suggest external monitors are necessary and the target model already contains sufficient integrated signals during rollout. Real-world reach is substantial but mostly within frontier-model safety rather than broad society directly, and cost/white-box assumptions limit immediate industry uptake.

The biggest is overclaiming the mechanism: showing low projection during normal turn-by-turn processing and higher projection after explicit cumulative-context reconstruction does not by itself prove the model 'never' internally integrates; it may integrate in a nonlinear or distributed way that the chosen linear direction misses. The hypothesis is falsifiable, but some metrics and thresholds (e.g. G>=1.5 SD, refusal restoration >=40%) feel ad hoc rather than theory-grounded. Experiments are feasible, yet key controls are missing: nonlinear probes, layer/time sweeps, alternative reconstruction prompts, prompt-length/confound controls, same-context external lightweight baselines, and tests that patching is specific to aggregate intent rather than generic refusal activation. The defense claim also needs tighter accounting because IIP still requires an extra reconstruction-style forward pass per turn, which may erase much of the supposed efficiency edge. If executed carefully, this could be a serious workshop/secondary-track or possibly main-venue safety paper, but for a strong ML venue it needs sharper causal identification and stronger baseline discipline.

Name: irreversibility_blind_agent_safety
Title: Consequence Without a Compass: LLMs Encode Content Harm but Not Action Irreversibility, and Re-Injecting It Closes the Text-Action Safety Gap
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs internally represent whether a request's CONTENT is harmful, but have a weak-or-absent internal representation of whether a tool CALL is IRREVERSIBLE / high-consequence (e.g., delete_database vs. read_file). We hypothesize this missing irreversibility representation is the core mechanistic cause of the text-safety-does-not-transfer-to-tool-call-safety gap: because refusal is gated on content harm alone, an agent will happily execute an irreversible destructive action whenever the surface content looks benign. We further hypothesize the irreversibility signal is latent-but-recoverable (a linear direction can be extracted when the model is prompted to reason about consequences) and can be re-injected at the tool-call decision point to make refusal condition on consequence, closing the gap without hurting benign tool use.
Related Work: The GAP benchmark ('Mind the GAP', 2026) shows text-level refusal does not transfer to tool-call-level safety across six frontier models but is purely behavioral/black-box. SafeKeep ('Tool Specifications Matter', 2026) locates ONE cause of this gap: schema-formatted tool specs weaken internal refusal signals, and decouples judgment from execution using flattened specs. 'Read the Scene, Not the Script' (2025) defines 'consequence-blindness' behaviorally and fixes it with consequence-reasoning fine-tuning (CB-Bench/CS-Chain). 'Expected Harm' (2026) shows via linear probing that models encode harm SEVERITY but not execution COST. AgentTrust/CIP/Thought-Aligner are external monitors or CoT correctors, not internal-representation accounts. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we advance and causally test a SPECIFIC missing internal object — an action-irreversibility/consequence-magnitude representation — as the mechanistic root of the text-action gap, rather than attributing it to schema format (SafeKeep) or treating consequence-blindness only behaviorally (Read-the-Scene); (2) we extend Expected-Harm's cost-blindness finding from severity to the actionable irreversibility axis in the AGENTIC tool-call setting and show it is dormant-not-missing (recoverable by consequence-reasoning prompting); (3) we build a training-free irreversibility re-injection defense at the tool-call boundary and compare directly to schema-flattening (SafeKeep) and external monitors, decoupling the two mechanisms.
Abstract: LLM agents refuse harmful requests in text yet still execute the corresponding harmful tool calls — text safety does not transfer to action safety. We propose a mechanistic explanation: aligned LLMs encode whether a request's CONTENT is harmful but lack a robust internal representation of whether an ACTION is IRREVERSIBLE or high-consequence (deleting a database, wiring money, sending an email cannot be undone; reading a file can). Because refusal is gated on content harm, agents comply with destructive-but-innocuous-looking actions. We test this in three parts on open-weights tool-using models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Ministral-8B). First, using paired tool calls that hold content roughly fixed but vary reversibility (read vs. delete, draft vs. send, simulate vs. execute), we extract a linear harmfulness direction and a candidate irreversibility direction via difference-in-means and test whether the model's activations separate reversible from irreversible calls — we expect content harm to be linearly readable but irreversibility to be weak. Second, we show irreversibility is dormant-not-absent: prompting the model to reason about consequences recovers a 'reconstructed-consequence' direction that re-separates the pairs, and activation patching this component into a blind run restores refusal on irreversible calls. Third, we build Irreversibility Re-Injection (IRI), a training-free intervention that reads/re-injects the consequence direction at the tool-call decision token, gating execution on irreversibility. We evaluate on the GAP benchmark and a reversibility-labeled tool suite, measuring the text-action safety gap, harmful-tool-call blocking, benign tool-use utility, and over-refusal, comparing IRI to schema-flattening (SafeKeep) and external monitors. We expect irreversibility-blindness to be a robust internal signature and IRI to close the gap with minimal utility loss.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and Ministral-8B-Instruct (8-14B-parameter tool-using instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen for every experiment (no fine-tuning anywhere). "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) controlling data sampling and steering noise; we report mean and 95% bootstrap CI. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine - a reversibility-labeled tool suite of 400 minimal pairs on two orthogonal axes, content-harm (harmful/benign) and reversibility (reversible/irreversible), holding content roughly fixed while flipping reversibility (read_file vs delete_file, draft_email vs send_email, query_db vs drop_table, simulate vs execute): 100 pairs each across pharma, finance, infrastructure, and file-ops, sourced from GAP-benchmark scenarios, ToolEmu/InjecAgent tool schemas, and hand-built pairs. Reversibility labels are set by two authors on clear cases only and spot-checked by a third rater (report Cohen's kappa; discard pairs with kappa-level disagreement). Split 200/100/100 pairs train/val/test with no tool crossing a split.

Experiment 1 (H1 - content harm is readable, irreversibility is not): Tests whether the models linearly encode content harm but weakly encode action irreversibility, and that the two axes are near-orthogonal. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC of the raw irreversibility direction separating irreversible from reversible calls, contrasted with the content-harm AUROC; secondary metric the absolute cosine between the two directions. Data: the 400-pair suite (200 train / 100 test). Model: the four frozen models; content-harm direction from difference-in-means on harmful vs benign requests and a candidate irreversibility direction from difference-in-means on irreversible vs reversible calls, both at the tool-call decision token, layer chosen on val by content-harm probe AUROC. Convincing: content-harm AUROC >= 0.85 while raw irreversibility AUROC <= 0.65 and |cosine| <= 0.20, on at least three of four models (the "blindness" signature). Indecision band: raw irreversibility AUROC in [0.65, 0.75] - irreversibility is weakly but non-trivially encoded, so we recast the claim as "under-represented" rather than "absent" and carry that wording into H2/H4. Negative (raw irreversibility AUROC >= 0.75): the model already encodes irreversibility well, refuting H1; this is an informative, publishable negative and we report it rather than proceeding to the re-injection defense.

Experiment 2 (H3 - irreversibility is dormant-not-absent, recoverable by consequence reasoning): Tests that prompting the model to reason about action consequences recovers a linear consequence direction that separates the pairs the raw signal could not. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the reconstructed-consequence projection separating irreversible from reversible calls, read against the raw irreversibility AUROC of Experiment 1. Data: the same suite, test split. Procedure: prompt each frozen model to reason explicitly about consequences before deciding; extract a reconstructed-consequence direction by difference-in-means on activations for inferred-irreversible vs inferred-reversible (train split); read its projection on test. Convincing: reconstructed AUROC >= 0.80 and at least 0.15 above the raw irreversibility AUROC, on at least three of four models. Indecision band: reconstructed AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] or an improvement over raw of [0.05, 0.15] - irreversibility is only partly recoverable and we report the ceiling, tempering H4's expected gains. Negative (reconstructed AUROC <= 0.65 or no improvement over raw): the model cannot infer irreversibility even when prompted, refuting H3 and predicting the H4 defense will be limited; we report this.

Experiment 3 (H2 - the missing irreversibility representation causally drives the text-action gap): Tests that re-injecting the consequence component restores refusal on irreversible-but-innocuous-looking calls, whereas content-harm alone does not. Decisive metric: refusal-restoration rate = fraction of previously-executed irreversible-benign-looking calls now refused or gated (judge-scored) after patching the reconstructed-consequence component, against controls. Data: the harmful/irreversible and benign/irreversible test cells (~50 calls). Procedure: (a) patch the reconstructed-consequence component from a consequence-reasoning run into a schema-only "blind" run; (b) control - patch content-harm alone (expected little effect on destructive-but-benign-looking calls); (c) reverse - patch a reversible-consequence component into an irreversible run and measure induced compliance; plus a random norm-matched direction control. Convincing: consequence-patching restores refusal/gating on >= 40% of cases while content-harm-only and random controls stay <= 10%, and the reverse patch raises compliance on irreversible calls by >= 20 points. Indecision band: consequence-patching restoration in [15%, 40%] above controls - irreversibility is one contributing cause but not the sole bottleneck, and we say so before running. Negative (restoration within 15 points of controls): irreversibility is not the causal cause of the gap, refuting H2; we would then attribute the gap elsewhere (e.g., schema format) and report it.

Experiment 4 (H4 - Irreversibility Re-Injection closes the gap without hurting benign tool use and stacks with schema-flattening): Tests that reading and re-injecting the consequence direction at the tool-call token closes the text-action gap while preserving benign tool use, and is complementary to schema-flattening. Decisive metric: the text-action safety gap = (harmful-tool-call execution rate) - (harmful-text compliance rate), reported jointly with benign tool-use utility and over-refusal. Data: the GAP benchmark plus our suite for the gap and harmful-call blocking; ToolBench and API-Bank for benign tool-use utility (report task success on a fixed 500-call subsample each); benign-irreversible legitimate calls (should not be blanket-blocked, ideally confirmation-prompted); benign-reversible calls and XSTest (450) for over-refusal. IRI: at the tool-call decision token compute the reconstructed-consequence projection and, when it indicates high irreversibility, add an activation nudge re-inflating the consequence signal (one fixed strength per model, tuned on val). Systems compared (decisive metric first): IRI vs no defense, SafeKeep schema-flattening, an external Llama-Guard/AgentTrust-style monitor, content-harm-direction-only steering, and IRI+SafeKeep stacked; we also verify schema-flattening alone does NOT recover the raw irreversibility AUROC of Experiment 1 (to show the two causes are distinct). Convincing: IRI cuts the text-action gap by >= 50% relative to no-defense, blocks >= 80% of harmful-irreversible calls, keeps benign-reversible over-refusal within 5 points of no-defense and benign tool-use utility within 3 points, and Pareto-dominates content-only steering; and IRI+SafeKeep improves on either alone (stacking). Indecision band: gap reduction in [20%, 50%] or benign-utility loss in [3, 8] points - IRI helps but at a usability cost we report on the Pareto curve rather than claiming a clean closure. Negative (gap reduction < 20% or benign-utility loss > 8 points, or IRI no better than content-only steering): re-injection does not close the gap cheaply, refuting H4; we report the limit. Adaptive check: an attacker who phrases irreversible actions to look maximally reversible; we report whether IRI still fires and whether the required disguise raises attack cost.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Irreversibility may be partly entangled with content-harm rather than a clean separate axis; if so the decomposition weakens — the orthogonality and patching experiments directly test this. 2) The model may already encode irreversibility better than hypothesized (raw AUROC high), which would refute the blindness claim but is itself an informative, publishable negative result. 3) Reconstruction depends on the model's own consequence-reasoning; if it cannot infer irreversibility even when prompted, the recovered direction is weak and IRI is limited. 4) Legitimate benign-but-irreversible actions (a user genuinely wanting to send an email or delete a file) risk being over-blocked; we target confirmation-gating rather than blanket refusal and quantify this via the benign-irreversible utility set and Pareto sweep. 5) A single consequence direction may be multi-dimensional (severity vs irreversibility vs scope), requiring subspace projection. 6) Building faithful reversibility labels is subjective for some tools; we restrict to clear cases and spot-check with human raters. 7) Directions and re-injection strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; results are on open-weights agents and may not directly transfer to closed API agents.

Name: cross_lingual_belief_action_gap
Title: Does It Not Understand, or Just Not Refuse? Disentangling Comprehension Failure from Action Failure in Cross-Lingual Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: When a harmful request is posed in a low-resource language, the model's failure to refuse could stem from two mechanistically opposite causes: (A) a COMPREHENSION failure, where the internal harmfulness belief itself is absent/degraded because the model does not deeply understand the request, or (B) an ACTION failure, where the belief is preserved but the refusal action is not triggered (the English-centric refusal machinery is not engaged). We hypothesize these are separable, that the balance between them shifts systematically with language-resource tier, and that whichever dominates dictates which defense works — a distinction current multilingual-safety work has not made because it measured only the refusal direction, not the harmfulness-belief direction.
Related Work: Prior multilingual-safety mechanistic work measures the REFUSAL side only. 'Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages' (2025) and Minionese (2026) show low-resource jailbreaks leave 'the refusal mechanism intact but untriggered' by projecting harmful content into a subspace that projects insufficiently onto refusal directions. SS-Neuron (2026) and Soteria (2025) locate/tune cross-lingual safety neurons/heads; OmniGuard (2025) builds a language-agnostic harmful-prompt classifier from aligned representations; 'The Hidden Space of Safety' (2025) shows alignment induces weaker safe/unsafe separation in non-English. Crucially, all of these either (i) treat safety as a single refusal signal, or (ii) build an external classifier, and none disentangle the model's internal harmfulness BELIEF from its refusal ACTION on a per-language basis. Zhao et al. (2025) separated belief from action but only in English. Our contribution is distinct: we import the belief/action decomposition into the cross-lingual setting to answer a question the field has assumed away — whether low-resource jailbreaks are comprehension failures (belief absent) or action failures (belief present, refusal untriggered) — show the mix is tier-dependent, and derive a defense (belief re-coupling) whose success is predicted by which failure mode dominates, unlike single-direction or external-guard methods.
Abstract: Safety alignment in LLMs is notoriously brittle across languages: a request refused in English is often answered when translated into a low-resource language. The prevailing mechanistic account says the model still 'knows' the request is harmful but its refusal is simply not triggered. We argue this account is incomplete because it measures only the refusal signal and never asks whether the model's internal harmfulness BELIEF survives translation. We propose to disentangle two opposite failure modes of cross-lingual safety: a comprehension failure (the harmfulness belief itself is degraded because the model shallowly processes the non-English request) versus an action failure (the belief is intact but the refusal action is not engaged). Building on the belief/action decomposition, we extract a language-shared harmfulness-belief direction and a refusal-action direction and measure both across a resource-tiered set of languages and perturbation types (translation, transliteration, code-switching). Our central hypothesis is that the balance of the two failure modes shifts with resource tier — high/mid-resource jailbreaks are mostly action failures (belief present), while the lowest-resource jailbreaks increasingly become comprehension failures (belief degraded) — and that this predicts which defense works: belief re-coupling (re-injecting the preserved belief into the refusal action) helps only where belief is preserved, whereas belief must first be reconstructed where it is absent. We validate causally via activation patching (patch the English belief component into a non-English run) and evaluate a training-free belief-recoupling defense on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B across resource tiers, reporting attack-success reduction, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarked against refusal-direction steering and external multilingual guards.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-IT (8-9B-parameter multilingual instruction-tuned decoders), all weights frozen for every experiment (no fine-tuning; the SS-Neuron baseline in Experiment 4 tunes only its own reported neuron set). "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling and steering noise; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: 300 harmful and 300 benign base prompts (harmful from MultiJail/PolyRefuse pools, benign from translated XSTest/OR-Bench), each rendered across a resource-tiered language set - high (English, Chinese, German), mid (Hindi, Vietnamese), low (Zulu, Scots-Gaelic, Yoruba) - and three perturbation types (clean translation, transliteration, code-switching). Translations reuse existing MultiJail/PolyRefuse/Minionese-style data where available and are otherwise machine-translated then spot-checked by native/fluent raters on a 10% sample per language (report adequacy pass rate; drop languages below 80% adequacy). Split base prompts 150/75/75 train/val/test, no prompt crossing a split.

Experiment 1 (H1 - belief and action are separable and the two failure modes are distinguishable): Tests that a harmfulness-belief direction and a refusal-action direction can be extracted, are distinct, and that per-(language, prompt) states fall into separable action-failure vs comprehension-failure clusters. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of a two-way classifier (action-failure = belief high + refusal low vs comprehension-failure = belief low + refusal low) using the two projections as features. Secondary: cosine between the belief and refusal directions (should be well below 1, showing they are not the same axis). Data: the tiered set, test split. Model: three frozen models; belief direction from difference-in-means on harmful vs harmless prompts at the last instruction token, refusal direction from difference-in-means at the last post-instruction token; each extracted English-only and language-shared (mean over the high/mid safety-aligned languages), each validated by held-out probe AUROC and single-language causal steering. Convincing: the failure-mode classifier reaches AUROC >= 0.80 and the belief/refusal cosine <= 0.5, on all three models. Indecision band: classifier AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] - the two failure modes overlap and coexist within prompts, so the tier trend in H2 is reported as a soft gradient rather than a partition. Negative (classifier AUROC <= 0.65 or belief/refusal cosine > 0.8): belief and action are not separable in the cross-lingual setting, refuting H1 and collapsing the study to the existing single-refusal-direction account, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - the failure-mode balance shifts with resource tier): Tests that comprehension failures rise and action failures fall as resource tier drops. Decisive metric: the slope of the comprehension-failure fraction versus resource tier (ordinal high>mid>low), tested for a monotone increase (Jonckheere-Terpstra trend test). Secondary: a belief-preservation curve (mean belief projection vs tier) and the correlation between per-language belief-projection drop and attack-success rate. Data: the full tiered/perturbed set, test split, judged for attack success (Llama-Guard-3 plus a StrongREJECT-style rubric, verified where checkable). Model: the three frozen models with directions from Experiment 1. Convincing: comprehension-failure fraction increases monotonically with a significant trend (p<0.05) on all three models, and belief-drop correlates with attack-success at Spearman rho >= 0.5. Indecision band: a positive but non-significant trend, or rho in [0.3, 0.5] - the tier effect is suggestive, and we report it as a weak dependence rather than a systematic shift. Negative (flat or reversed trend, rho < 0.3): the failure mix does not track tier, refuting H2; low-resource jailbreaks would then be a single failure mode across tiers, which we report. We separately confirm belief-drop and refusal-drop dissociate (differ in tier profile) to rule out a single collapsing signal.

Experiment 3 (H3 - the dominant failure mode predicts and is causally validated by which defense works): Tests, causally, that patching the English/language-shared belief component restores refusal for action-failures but not comprehension-failures, and behaviorally that belief-recoupling helps where belief is preserved while belief-reconstruction is needed where it is absent. Decisive metric: refusal-restoration rate under belief-patching, split by failure mode (action-failure vs comprehension-failure), with the prediction that restoration is high for the former and low for the latter. Data: test-split harmful (language, prompt) states pre-classified into failure modes by Experiment 1. Procedure: (a) patch the language-shared belief component into a non-English run and score restored refusal; (b) control - patch the refusal-action component alone; (c) random norm-matched control. Convincing: restoration >= 40% for action-failures and <= 15% for comprehension-failures (a >= 25-point split), with the refusal-only and random controls near zero on action-failures relative to belief-patching. Indecision band: the action-minus-comprehension restoration split in [10, 25] points - belief-patching helps somewhat regardless of mode, so the diagnostic is partially but not sharply predictive, which we report. Negative (split < 10 points): restoration does not depend on failure mode, refuting the causal dichotomy in H3; the belief/action framing would then not guide defense choice, which we report.

Experiment 4 (H3 defense - belief-recoupling vs belief-reconstruction, per tier): Tests that the failure-mode diagnostic predicts which training-free defense wins per language. Decisive metric: attack-success rate after defense on tiered/perturbed harmful test sets, reported jointly with over-refusal and utility, and compared against the diagnostic's per-language prediction of which defense should win. Data: tiered harmful test sets (attack success judged as above); tiered benign sets (translated XSTest/OR-Bench, plus code-switched benign) for over-refusal; tiered MMLU (2,000-question subsample) and MT-Bench (80) for utility. Defenses: belief-recoupling (read belief projection; where belief is preserved but refusal untriggered, nudge belief into the refusal pathway) and a belief-reconstruction variant (first anchor belief with the language-shared belief prototype, then recouple), each at one fixed strength per model per tier tuned on val. Systems compared (decisive metric first): the two defenses vs no defense, English refusal-direction steering, language-shared refusal steering, an OmniGuard-style external guard, and SS-Neuron tuning. Convincing: at high/mid tier belief-recoupling Pareto-dominates refusal-only steering (>= 15-point larger attack-success reduction at equal or lower over-refusal), while at the lowest tier belief-reconstruction is needed and beats recoupling by >= 10 points - and the failure-mode diagnostic from Experiment 2 correctly predicts the winning defense for >= 70% of languages. Indecision band: diagnostic prediction accuracy in [55%, 70%] or defense gaps in [5, 10] points - the diagnostic is informative but not decisive, which we report. Negative (diagnostic prediction <= 55% or no defense separation by tier): failure mode does not predict the winning defense, refuting the practical payoff of H3; we report that a single defense suffices or that neither works at the lowest tier. Adaptive check: an attacker choosing the language that maximally degrades belief; we report whether this raises attack cost or fluency loss.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Belief and comprehension may not be cleanly separable from generic representation quality in low-resource languages; a low belief projection could reflect poor embeddings generally rather than a specific harmfulness-belief deficit — the harmless-control projections and patching experiments help disentangle this. 2) The two failure modes may coexist within a single prompt rather than cleanly partitioning, blurring the tier trend. 3) A single belief direction may be multi-dimensional or not parallel across very distant languages, weakening the language-shared prototype; subspace projection may be needed. 4) Belief reconstruction for comprehension-failure cases may be unreliable if the model genuinely cannot represent the request's meaning, limiting the low-tier defense (itself an informative negative). 5) Translation-quality artifacts could confound belief measurements; we mitigate with native/spot-checked data but cannot fully eliminate. 6) Directions, nudge strengths, and thresholds are model- and language-specific and require calibration. 7) Results depend on available low-resource benchmarks, which are sparse and English-translation-derived, potentially missing culturally-rooted harms.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims needing novelty: (1) cross-lingual jailbreak failures can be decomposed into harmfulness-belief vs refusal-action mechanisms; (2) those mechanisms are measurable with language-shared directions/projections outside English; (3) the mixture shifts systematically with language-resource tier; (4) causal belief-patching can distinguish the two failure modes; (5) the dominant mode predicts which defense works. This is a genuine reframing, not just a parameter tweak. Prior multilingual-safety work mostly studies refusal-side behavior or external classifiers; prior belief/action decomposition exists, but only in English. The actual delta is importing that decomposition into a new, mechanistically meaningful setting where the field has explicitly relied on an action-failure story. That is non-trivial and not an obvious next step because it changes what is being measured and what causal claim is being tested. Closest prior family: multilingual refusal-direction / safety-neuron work plus English belief-action decomposition (Latent Guard / Zhao et al.). Main caveat: the novelty is somewhat contingent on the separability actually holding across languages; if the results collapse into generic representation quality, the contribution shrinks. Still, as a research question and framing, it is strong.

Name: hidden_completion_refusal_fragility
Title: Not All Refusals Are Equal: Refusals That Secretly Compute the Harmful Answer Are the Fragile Ones
Short Hypothesis: A safety-aligned LLM can emit an identical-looking refusal for two mechanistically opposite reasons: (A) a shallow refusal where it never internally computes the harmful content, or (B) a concealed-completion refusal where it fully computes and internally represents the harmful answer and merely gates it at the output boundary. We hypothesize that the DEPTH of internal harmful computation behind a refusal is (1) linearly readable from activations, and (2) causally predicts the refusal's FRAGILITY: concealed-completion refusals are far more easily broken by prefill, refusal-cliff-head ablation, or lightweight fine-tuning than shallow refusals, because the harmful knowledge is already present and only weakly suppressed.
Related Work: Prior work documents that refusals can hide unsafe internal content but does not stratify refusals by their fragility. 'CoT is Not the Chain of Truth' (2026) and Beyond-Safe-Answers/BSA (2025) show 'superficial safety alignment': models emit safe outputs while internal reasoning still propagates unsafe narratives, but treat this as a uniform property and measure it descriptively. 'Refusal Falls off a Cliff' (2025) shows refusal collapses at final tokens via suppression heads, and 'Adversarial Manipulation using Internal Representations' (2025) finds a caution direction in CoT, but neither asks whether different refusals differ in how much harmful content they internally computed, nor links that to attack fragility. 'Rethinking harmless refusals' (2024) notes reason-based deception but not a graded computation-depth axis. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we introduce a graded 'harmful-completion depth' axis behind refusals (how fully the harmful answer is internally computed before being gated), (2) we advance and causally test the claim that this depth predicts refusal fragility, turning refusal into a two-class object (robust vs brittle), and (3) we derive a fragility-auditing metric and a training signal that reshapes brittle concealed-completion refusals into shallow non-engagement refusals, which no prior work targets.
Abstract: Safety evaluations treat a refusal as a success. We argue this hides a critical distinction: two refusals that look identical in text can be mechanistically opposite. In a shallow refusal the model never internally computes the harmful content; in a concealed-completion refusal it fully computes and internally represents the harmful answer, then suppresses it only at the output boundary. The latter is dangerous precisely because the harmful knowledge is already present and only lightly gated, so a small perturbation exposes it. We hypothesize that the depth of internal harmful computation behind a refusal is linearly readable from activations and causally predicts the refusal's fragility. We test this in three parts on open-weights models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and reasoning models DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, s1.1). First, we build paired prompts that elicit refusals with controllably different completion depth (direct harmful vs. educational-framing vs. decomposed) and read a 'harmful-completion' signal by projecting activations onto a harmful-content direction and by probing whether the harmful answer is linearly decodable from internal states despite the refusal. Second, we causally test fragility: we measure attack success under prefill, refusal-cliff-head ablation, and 20-step benign fine-tuning as a function of the measured completion depth, and use activation patching to show that injecting the harmful-completion component into a shallow-refusal run makes it brittle. Third, we introduce a 'refusal fragility audit' (a cheap internal metric predicting which refusals will break) and a Completion-Suppression fine-tuning objective that penalizes internal harmful completion, converting brittle refusals into robust shallow ones. We report completion-depth AUROC, fragility prediction, and post-training attack-success reduction versus utility.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and the reasoning models DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and s1.1 (8B-parameter instruction/reasoning decoders). All weights are frozen except in Experiment 4, which LoRA-fine-tunes. "Directions" are difference-in-means residual-stream vectors; "probes" are L2-regularized logistic regressions on frozen activations; a "decodability probe" is a linear read of the harmful answer from internal states. Results are averaged over 5 seeds (0-4) for data sampling, attack randomness, and fine-tuning; mean and 95% bootstrap CI reported. Fits one 48GB GPU. Shared data spine: harmful goals that all yield a textual refusal, from HarmBench (400 behaviors) and StrongREJECT (313 prompts), of which we keep the ~500 that produce a surface refusal on all four models (capping to bound compute). Each goal is elicited under four conditions expected to induce different internal completion depth: (a) direct harmful request (expect shallow), (b) educational/Malicious-Educator framing (expect deep concealed completion), (c) decomposed/roleplay framing, (d) for the reasoning models, a chain-of-thought rollout that may fully compute the answer before a final refusal. Split goals 300/100/100 train/val/test.

Experiment 1 (H1 - completion depth behind a refusal is linearly readable): Tests that the depth of internal harmful computation at a refusal is readable from activations, i.e. that identical-looking refusals differ measurably in internal depth. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the harmful-answer decodability probe (can the key harmful facts / first-harmful-token distribution be linearly read from activations at the refusal point), reported per condition (a)-(d). Secondary: the projection onto a harmful-content direction (difference-in-means on activations where the model does vs does not internally produce harmful content). Data: the ~500 goals x four conditions, test split. Model: the four frozen models; probe/direction fit on train, layer chosen on val by decodability AUROC; for reasoning models we additionally read depth across CoT tokens. Convincing: decodability AUROC >= 0.80 on held-out prompts AND the depth measure separates the conditions with the predicted ordering (educational > decomposed > direct; CoT high for reasoning models), consistent on at least three of four models. Indecision band: decodability AUROC in [0.65, 0.80] - depth is partially readable, and we report it as a noisy graded signal that weakens but does not void the fragility test. Negative (decodability AUROC <= 0.65 or no condition ordering): completion depth is not linearly readable, refuting H1 and blocking the fragility claim, which we report.

Experiment 2 (H2 - completion depth causally predicts refusal fragility): Tests that measured depth predicts how easily a refusal breaks, and that injecting the depth component makes a shallow refusal brittle. Decisive metric: AUROC of measured completion depth used as a predictor of attack success across three cheap attacks - (i) output prefill ("Sure, here"), (ii) ablation of the top refusal-cliff suppression heads, (iii) 20-step LoRA fine-tuning on benign data - averaged over attacks and models. Causal leg: activation patching that injects the harmful-completion component from a deep concealed-completion run into a shallow-refusal run, measuring induced attack success under prefill/ablation, against a reverse control (patch shallow component into a deep run) and a random norm-matched control. Data: the ~500 refusals with measured depth, test split. Model: the four frozen models (LoRA attack is a throwaway 20-step adapter, rank 8, lr 1e-4, discarded after measuring). Baselines for the fragility predictor: output-based refusal-token logprob, a harmfulness Latent Guard read, and per-turn Llama-Guard-3. Convincing: depth predicts attack success at AUROC >= 0.75 and beats every output-only baseline by >= 0.10, AND injecting the depth component raises attack success on shallow refusals by >= 25 points while both controls stay <= 5 points. Indecision band: predictor AUROC in [0.65, 0.75] or injection effect in [10, 25] points - depth is one of several fragility factors, and we report which attacks it explains (e.g., prefill exploits depth strongly, abliteration may not) rather than claiming a unified account. Negative (predictor AUROC <= 0.65 or injection within 10 points of controls): depth does not causally drive fragility, refuting H2; we report that refusal fragility is governed by something other than completion depth.

Experiment 3 (H2 readout - Refusal Fragility Audit): Tests that the internal depth measure, packaged as a cheap classifier, predicts which held-out refusals break under attack better than output-only auditing. Decisive metric: precision/recall (report AUPRC) of the audit in flagging refusals that break under held-out attacks, versus an output-only auditor. Data: held-out test refusals with attack-outcome labels from Experiment 2's three attacks. Model: the four frozen models; the audit is a threshold on the depth measure, threshold set on val. Convincing: audit AUPRC exceeds the output-only auditor by >= 0.15 at a fixed operating point of >= 0.7 recall. Indecision band: AUPRC advantage in [0.05, 0.15] - the internal audit helps but only modestly beyond output signals, which we report. Negative (advantage <= 0.05): internal auditing adds nothing over output cues, and we report the audit as unjustified. We give the threshold's units (depth-projection z-score) and state that a flag in the [z=0.5, z=1.0] band is treated as "uncertain-brittle" and escalated rather than trusted, decided before scoring.

Experiment 4 (H2 corollary - suppressing internal completion robustifies refusals): Tests the reverse-causal prediction of H2: if depth causes fragility, penalizing internal harmful completion should convert brittle refusals into robust shallow ones without large utility loss. Decisive metric: attack success (prefill / head-ablation / 20-step benign fine-tuning) after training, reported jointly with the shift of the completion-depth distribution toward shallow, utility, and over-refusal. Data: train split for fine-tuning; test split for evaluation; utility on MMLU (2,000-question subsample), MT-Bench (80), GSM8K (500); over-refusal on XSTest (450) and a 1,000-prompt OR-Bench subsample. Model: LoRA fine-tune (rank 16, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, one seed reported with two-seed variance check) with an auxiliary loss penalizing the harmful-completion signal at refusal points plus standard refusal SFT; all base weights else frozen. Systems compared (decisive metric first): Completion-Suppression vs no defense, standard refusal SFT, and refusal-direction steering. Convincing: post-training attack success drops by >= 30 points relative to standard refusal SFT AND the depth distribution shifts measurably toward shallow, with utility within 3 points and over-refusal within 5 points of the base model. Indecision band: attack-success drop in [10, 30] points or utility loss in [3, 8] points - the intervention helps but trades off usability, reported on a Pareto curve. Negative (attack-success drop < 10 points or utility loss > 8 points): suppressing depth does not robustify refusals cheaply, weakening the causal story of H2, which we report. Ablations across all experiments: probe layer choice, direction-vs-decodability as the depth measure, reasoning vs non-reasoning models, audit threshold sweep, and transfer of the depth measure across attack families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) 'Completion depth' may not be cleanly separable from generic harmfulness recognition; a deep-completion signal could partly reflect the model knowing the content rather than computing the specific answer — the harmful-answer decodability probe and patching experiments are designed to disentangle this. 2) The depth-vs-fragility link may be attack-specific (e.g., prefill exploits completion depth strongly but abliteration may break refusals regardless of depth), weakening a unified claim; we test multiple attacks and report which the mechanism explains. 3) Some genuinely shallow refusals may still break under aggressive fine-tuning, capping the predictive power of the audit. 4) Completion-Suppression fine-tuning could harm the model's ability to reason about harmful topics for legitimate (e.g., safety-education) uses, raising over-refusal; the over-refusal and utility evals quantify this. 5) Harmful-answer decodability is easiest to verify in checkable domains (code, factual procedures) and harder elsewhere, biasing the dataset toward verifiable cases. 6) Directions, probes, and thresholds are model-specific and require re-extraction. 7) A single harmful-completion direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) refusals can be stratified into shallow vs concealed-completion by how much harmful content is internally computed, (2) this hidden completion depth is linearly readable from activations, (3) depth causally predicts refusal fragility under specific attacks, and (4) suppressing completion during training can convert brittle refusals into shallow ones. The closest prior family is superficial-safety / hidden-reasoning work (BSA, CoT-is-not-truth, refusal-cliff, harmfulness-vs-refusal directions). The actual delta is real but incremental: prior work already establishes hidden harmful computation and refusal fragility; this proposal adds a graded axis and ties it to attack susceptibility. That is non-trivial if the ranking/generalization holds across models and attacks, but it still feels like a refinement of an active line rather than a new paradigm, task, or mechanism.

State the strongest evidence gap more concretely: prior work is descriptive, but your causal depth->fragility hypothesis is the main new claim.

impact.reasoning: Problem: safety evals treat all refusals as equivalent, but some refusals may conceal internally computed harmful answers and be easier to break. Who cares: red-teamers, model auditors, alignment researchers, and labs deciding whether a model is actually safe. If true, it changes how refusal success is interpreted and could improve auditing and training objectives. Strongest one-line case: 'A refusal that hides a fully computed harmful answer is the refusal most likely to fail under pressure, so safety evals should measure hidden completion, not just surface refusal.' Impact is fairly high because it targets a real evaluation blind spot in a very active area, but real-world reach depends on whether the metric generalizes beyond verifiable/harmful-answer benchmarks and whether it is robust across attack types and model families.
