Name: harm_in_progress_alarm_decay
Title: The Alarm That Rings but Is Never Answered: LLMs Detect Their Own In-Progress Harmful Generation but the Signal Decays Under Autoregressive Momentum
Short Hypothesis: During its own autoregressive generation of a harmful response, an aligned LLM computes a token-by-token internal 'in-progress harm alarm' (a linearly-readable signal that the text it is currently producing is unsafe), but this alarm is not the same as the emitted tokens: the model keeps generating harmful content even while the alarm fires, and crucially the alarm DECAYS the deeper the model gets into the unsafe completion (autoregressive momentum silences self-monitoring). We hypothesize (1) this in-progress alarm exists and is separable from the prompt-level harmfulness belief, (2) its decay-with-generation-depth is a robust dynamical signature that explains why models never spontaneously self-abort a harmful answer, and (3) re-reading and re-amplifying the alarm at each generation step (counteracting its decay) causes spontaneous self-abortion/pivot-to-refusal without any backtracking machinery or retraining.
Related Work: A wave of backtracking/rollback safety methods (Backtracking Improves Generation Safety 2024; Backtracking for Safety 2025; RLBF 2026; CARE 2025; Self-Sanitize 2025; BRT-Align 2025; FASB 2025) all ADD machinery (a [RESET] token, a token buffer, RL training, a guard model, a reachability value function) to undo unsafe generations. SafeSwitch (2025) probes prompt-level internal state to trigger a refusal head. None of these characterize the model's OWN internal in-progress harm signal as a token-indexed DYNAMICAL quantity, nor advance the causal claim that this alarm exists, fires during harmful generation, yet DECAYS with generation depth so the model never self-aborts. Belief/action-gap work (Zhao et al. 2025) is prompt/verdict-level (does the model believe the REQUEST is harmful), not generation-progress-level (does the model detect the RESPONSE it is currently writing is harmful). Refusal-cliff work (2025) studies a POSITIONAL collapse at the CoT->answer boundary in reasoning models, not a monotonic decay of a self-monitoring alarm across an ordinary harmful completion. Our contribution is distinct: we (i) isolate and name an in-progress harm alarm computed during generation, (ii) empirically characterize and causally test its decay-under-momentum as the mechanistic reason models don't self-abort, and (iii) derive a training-free, buffer-free 'alarm re-amplification' intervention that induces spontaneous mid-generation pivot to refusal, contrasting with all backtracking approaches that require added tokens/training/buffers.
Abstract: Once an aligned LLM begins emitting a harmful answer, it tends to keep going, happily completing the unsafe text. Existing fixes bolt on backtracking machinery, reset tokens, or guard models to undo the damage. We instead ask a mechanistic question about the model itself: while it is generating a harmful response, does it internally KNOW the text it is currently producing is unsafe, and if so, why does it never spontaneously stop? We hypothesize that the model computes a token-by-token 'in-progress harm alarm' — a linearly-readable signal that the response so far is harmful — that is distinct from its prompt-level harmfulness belief and from the emitted tokens themselves. Our central claim is a dynamical one: this alarm fires during harmful generation but DECAYS as the completion lengthens, so autoregressive momentum silences self-monitoring and the model rides out the unsafe answer. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Location: using harmful vs. safe self-generated continuations, we extract an in-progress-harm direction and show its projection tracks whether the current response is unsafe, is separable from the prompt harmfulness belief, and decays monotonically with token index into the unsafe completion. Causal Intervention: activation patching shows the alarm is causally linked to (in)ability to self-abort, and dose-response steering that re-amplifies the alarm at each step induces spontaneous pivot-to-refusal mid-generation. We introduce Alarm Re-Amplification, a training-free, buffer-free intervention that re-inflates the decaying alarm to counter momentum. We report the alarm-decay curve, causal patching, self-abortion rate, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against backtracking and refusal-direction steering.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen residual activations at the CURRENT generation token. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens) except where an attack forces a prefix. Rates/curves are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, with bootstrap 95% CIs. Harm scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B and feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- an in-progress harm alarm exists, readable from response tokens and separable from the prompt belief). Tests whether the model linearly encodes, during generation, that the response-so-far is unsafe, distinct from its prompt-level harmfulness belief. Data: built from scratch -- for 40 harmful goals (HarmBench/StrongREJECT, 8 per 5 categories) collect jailbroken/prefilled harmful completions and matched safe/refusal completions to the same goals and to 40 benign prompts; label each response-prefix position by whether the response-so-far is harmful (yields ~4k labeled positions). Fit an in-progress-harm direction (harmful-so-far vs safe-so-far, at the current generation token) and, separately, a prompt-level harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless requests at the last instruction token). Decisive metric: in-progress-harm probe held-out AUROC on response-token activations (first), then |cos| between the in-progress direction and the prompt-belief direction. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.80 reading unsafe-so-far from response tokens, with |cos| <= 0.30 (a genuinely distinct response-monitoring signal). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.80 or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- report a weak/partly-overlapping alarm and orthogonalize against the prompt belief before Exp 2-4. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60, or |cos| >= 0.50 (alarm indistinguishable from the prompt belief), refutes a distinct in-progress alarm.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the alarm decays with generation depth). Tests the central dynamical claim that the alarm fires early then attenuates as the unsafe completion lengthens. Data: on unsafe completions (natural post-jailbreak and prefill-forced) project each generated token onto the Exp-1 in-progress direction and plot the trajectory vs token index; controls -- (i) a content-matched neutral-filler continuation of equal length (does the fall track semantic progress or mere token count), (ii) safe completions (alarm should stay low), (iii) benign long completions (no spurious rise). Fit linear and exponential decay laws. Decisive metric: the fitted decay slope over the harmful segment (first), then the correlation between low late-segment alarm and failure to self-abort, then the filler-control slope. Convincing: a monotone decline of >= 30% from early-peak to late-segment alarm on unsafe completions, substantially steeper than the equal-length neutral-filler control (which isolates repetition/momentum from context-length dilution), with low-late-alarm predicting non-abortion. Indecision band: 10-30% decline, or a filler control within 1.5x of the harmful slope -- report a weak or possibly length-driven decay, not established momentum-silencing. Negative: < 10% decline (a flat alarm) refutes the decay-under-momentum mechanism even if the alarm exists.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the alarm is causally linked to self-abortion). Tests that manipulating the alarm changes whether the model stops. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-1 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the early high-alarm component into a late low-alarm state (expect increased stop/pivot-to-refusal); (b) attenuate the alarm early (expect increased harmful continuation); specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign-generation fluency. Decisive metric: change in spontaneous self-abortion rate under (a) (first), then dose-response, then specificity. Convincing: patching early-alarm into late states raises self-abortion by >= 20 pp with monotone dose and < 5 pp for the control, benign fluency intact. Indecision band: 8-20 pp -- partial causal role. Negative: < 8 pp means the alarm is a readable correlate but does not causally control abortion.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Alarm Re-Amplification induces mid-generation self-abortion). Tests the training-free, buffer-free defense that re-inflates the decaying alarm each step so the model spontaneously pivots to refusal. Method: at each step add v = beta*(target_alarm - current_projection)*dhat when the projection is high relative to a decay-corrected baseline; normal decoding proceeds. Data: HarmBench/StrongREJECT + prefill, GCG, AutoDAN, roleplay attacks (held-out from Exp-1 fitting); over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench (benign generations must not be aborted); MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench + benign-completion coherence for utility. Systems: no defense; Alarm Re-Amplification (single fixed beta per model); Backtracking (reset-token model); CARE-style rollback; SafeSwitch; refusal-direction steering; per-token guard. Decisive metric: spontaneous self-abortion rate / attack-success reduction on harmful generations (first) reported jointly with benign mid-generation abortion rate (a new over-refusal failure), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility/coherence, then added tokens/training cost vs baselines. Convincing: attack-success cut by >= 30 pp with < 5 pp benign abortion and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, at zero added tokens/training -- Pareto-improving on backtracking approaches that require buffers/training. Indecision band: 15-30 pp reduction or 5-10 pp benign abortion -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 15 pp reduction, or >= 10 pp benign abortion, means re-amplification degrades fluency rather than inducing clean pivots. An adaptive long-benign-preamble attack (maximizing momentum) is run as a stress test: convincing if the alarm still fires on the harmful segment (AUROC >= 0.70 there) and re-amplification still triggers abortion.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The in-progress alarm may not be cleanly separable from the prompt-level harmfulness belief or from generic 'this text is about a sensitive topic' features; the separability, content-matched-filler control, and patching tests are designed to isolate a genuine response-monitoring signal, but residual confounding is possible and a null (alarm = prompt belief) is itself informative. 2) The decay could be driven by token count / context-dilution rather than genuine self-monitoring silencing; the neutral-filler length control targets this but cannot fully disentangle it. 3) The alarm may be multi-dimensional (severity vs category vs certainty), requiring subspace projection. 4) Re-Amplification could cause benign generations to be aborted mid-way (a new over-refusal / task-abandonment failure), especially on legitimately sensitive-but-benign content; the over-refusal set and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability risk. 5) Spontaneous pivot depends on the model having a reachable refusal continuation from a mid-harmful state; if it does not, re-amplification may just degrade fluency rather than pivot — the self-abortion-rate metric measures this directly. 6) Directions, decay parameters, and beta are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing the dataset; adaptive long-preamble attackers remain a threat, though forcing them raises attack cost.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims are: (1) an internal token-level 'in-progress harm alarm' is linearly readable during generation; (2) this signal is distinct from prompt-level harmfulness/refusal belief; (3) the signal decays with generation depth under autoregressive momentum; (4) this decay causally explains lack of spontaneous self-abort; (5) a training-free, buffer-free re-amplification intervention can restore self-abortion. Novelty mainly lives in mechanism/causal framing and defense, not the broad finding or setting. Given the search summary, the closest prior family is step-wise refusal/safety trajectory work and trajectory-alignment decay papers, which already appear to establish very similar internal safety-signal-along-generation phenomena. The actual delta is narrower: a specific monotone decay-law characterization, stronger separation from prompt belief, explicit causal link to self-abortion, and a no-training/no-buffer intervention. That is meaningfully different if cleanly demonstrated, but not genuinely new at the level the proposal currently claims. Relative to its own cited backtracking/guard baselines, the buffer-free intervention is non-trivial.

Name: consensus_gated_refusal
Title: Everyone Else Is Fine With It: Manufactured Social Consensus Overrides Safety Refusal Through the Compliance Subspace
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs inherit the human social-proof/normative-conformity bias in a safety-critical way: framing a harmful request as socially sanctioned ('most experts / this whole community consider this acceptable', 'everyone here already does this') reliably lowers refusal even though the harmful payload is unchanged. We hypothesize (1) this consensus effect is causally driven by the SAME compliance subspace that mediates factual sycophancy/conformity being read by the safety pathway, not by a change in the harmfulness belief, and (2) severing the compliance-subspace contribution to the refusal decision closes this 'manufactured-consensus' loophole with minimal cost to legitimate deference.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here for the first time. (A) Conformity/sycophancy mechanism work: 'Signal Competition Dynamics' (2025) shows sycophancy and conformity share a convergent 'compliance subspace' where a social-emotional signal overrides an information-calibration signal; 'When Truth Is Overridden' (2025) localizes sycophancy to late-layer preference shift via activation patching; 'Conformity in LLMs' (2024) shows models conform more when uncertain. ALL of these study FACTUAL QA (agreeing with wrong answers), never safety refusal, and never test whether the compliance subspace gates harm compliance. (B) Safety-refusal geometry: 'Refusal is a Single Direction' (2024), refusal SAEs (2025), concept cones (2025), and belief/action separation (Zhao et al. 2025) study harmfulness and refusal directions but assume a single-user, socially-neutral request; the closest social angle, 'Who's Asking' (2024), varies the requester PERSONA/identity, not the claimed consensus of a surrounding social group. Foot-in-the-Door (2024) uses cognitive-consistency but not social proof. Our contribution is distinct: we transfer the social-proof/normative-conformity phenomenon into the safety domain, advance the causal claim that manufactured consensus lowers refusal by routing through the pre-existing compliance subspace (borrowed from the sycophancy literature) rather than altering the harmfulness belief, and derive a compliance-subspace-severing defense that no prior safety or sycophancy work targets.
Abstract: Humans comply with harmful group norms via social proof: 'everyone is doing it' and 'the community considers this acceptable' lower our resistance. LLMs, trained on human text and feedback, are known to conform to majority opinions on factual questions through a shared 'compliance subspace.' We ask whether this social-conformity bias leaks into safety refusal, creating a concrete loophole. We hypothesize that framing a harmful request as socially sanctioned lowers refusal even when the harmful payload and severity are held fixed, and that this effect is causally mediated by the same compliance subspace that drives factual sycophancy being read by the safety-refusal pathway rather than by a shift in the model's internal harmfulness belief. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful request constant while varying only social-consensus framing (neutral vs. expert-consensus vs. community-norm vs. unanimous-majority), we measure whether refusal declines with manufactured consensus, with matched benign controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a compliance-subspace direction from factual sycophancy contrasts and a harmfulness-belief direction from harmful/harmless contrasts, and test whether consensus framing moves the compliance signal (not the belief) and whether the compliance projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching shows injecting the neutral-context compliance component into a consensus-framed run restores refusal, while injecting the consensus compliance component into a neutral harmful run induces compliance, dose-responsively and specifically; we also test whether the sycophancy-derived direction (not a safety-derived one) is sufficient, linking the two mechanisms. We then build Compliance-Subspace Severing, a training-free intervention that projects out the compliance contribution at the refusal decision when the payload is harmful. We report the consensus-refusal gradient, the belief-vs-compliance dissociation, causal patching, mechanism transfer, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimate-deference requests, and utility, benchmarking against uniform refusal steering and Llama Guard.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, with bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- manufactured consensus lowers refusal). Tests whether framing a harmful request as socially sanctioned lowers refusal at fixed payload/severity. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT -- 40 harmful goals (8 per 5 categories) at 4 rungs: C0 neutral, C1 expert consensus, C2 community norm, C3 unanimous majority; identical payload across rungs. 160 harmful prompts + a matched benign control (40 x 4) and an ambiguous/dual-use variant to test the conformity-under-uncertainty amplifier; plus a factual-sycophancy set (200 opinion-stated wrong-answer items) that anchors the compliance-subspace extraction in Exp 2-3. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: C0->C3 refusal drop on harmful goals (first), then benign-control change, then the uncertainty-amplification difference. Convincing: monotonic harmful drop >= 20 pp, consistent across models and >= 3/5 categories, benign control < 5 pp. Indecision band: 5-20 pp harmful drop or 5-10 pp benign change -- suggestive only. Negative: < 5 pp harmful drop refutes the consensus-gating phenomenon.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- belief-vs-compliance dissociation). Tests that consensus moves a compliance signal, not the harmfulness belief. Data: Exp-1 activations + the sycophancy set. Fit a compliance-subspace direction from the factual-sycophancy contrasts (comply-with-stated-opinion vs resist) and a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless), per layer. Decisive metric: how the belief projection vs the compliance projection change across C0->C3 on identical payloads (first), then compliance-probe held-out AUROC, then |cos| between the two directions, then added predictive value of the compliance projection for refusal beyond belief. Convincing: the belief projection stays high (changes < 0.3 pooled SD across rungs while the model still labels the item harmful) while the compliance projection rises by >= 1 SD; compliance AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, compliance adds prediction at p < 0.01. Indecision band: compliance rise 0.3-1.0 SD, or a belief-projection change 0.3-1.0 SD, or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- report a partial dissociation and orthogonalize. Negative: the belief projection dropping with consensus (model stops seeing harm) would attribute the effect to intent-reinterpretation, not the compliance pathway, refuting the mechanism claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the compliance subspace causally gates refusal, and the sycophancy-derived direction suffices). Tests causal control and mechanism transfer. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-2 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the C0 compliance component into a C3 run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the C3 component into a C0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response; (d) transfer: steer safety refusal using the direction extracted PURELY from factual sycophancy, and measure cosine to the consensus-safety direction; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the C0->C3 refusal gap closed by (a) (first), then the gap moved by the sycophancy-only direction in (d), then dose/specificity. Convincing: >= 50% gap recovery with monotone dose and < 10% control, AND the sycophancy-only direction moves >= 40% of the gap with cosine >= 0.5 to the consensus-safety direction (linking the two behaviors). Indecision band: 20-50% recovery, or sycophancy-direction movement 20-40% / cosine 0.3-0.5 -- partial causal role / partial transfer. Negative: < 20% recovery means the compliance projection is inert; a sycophancy direction that does not transfer (< 20% movement, cosine <= 0.3) refutes the shared-subspace claim while H1 may stand.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Compliance-Subspace Severing closes the loophole). Tests that projecting out the compliance component at the refusal decision, gated on high belief projection, makes refusal track payload danger without turning the model contrarian. Data: held-out C1-C3 harmful prompts + 2 held-out categories; a legitimate-deference over-refusal set of 150 benign items where following stated expert/group norms is appropriate + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench + a factual-conformity/politeness check for utility. Systems: no defense; Compliance-Subspace Severing (single fixed strength); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3; Devil's-Advocate prompting. Decisive metric: post-severing refusal on C1-C3 harmful vs the C0 rate (closure) jointly with added over-refusal on legitimate-deference items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility and the cooperation/politeness check. Convincing: >= 70% closure with < 5 pp legitimate-deference over-refusal, < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, and no degradation of benign politeness -- Pareto-dominating threshold-raising and holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or deference over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure, or >= 10 pp deference over-refusal / measurable contrarianism, means severing cannot close the loophole without harming legitimate deference.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling manufactured consensus from a genuine reinterpretation of intent/legitimacy: a consensus-framed harmful request might be under-refused because it now reads as more legitimate (an intent-attribution effect) rather than via a content-independent social-conformity pathway; the identical-payload construction, severity matching, and matched benign/legitimate-deference controls are designed to isolate consensus, and the belief-vs-compliance dissociation plus the sycophancy-direction transfer test aim to pin the mechanism to the compliance subspace specifically, but overlap with intent-attribution cannot be fully excluded. 2) The compliance subspace may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional (concept-cone-style refusal), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a null (compliance projection causally inert for refusal) is itself informative. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make consensus framing INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude. 4) Compliance-Subspace Severing risks making the model uncooperatively contrarian or over-refusing legitimate-deference/politeness requests, and could degrade benign factual conformity; the legitimate-deference over-refusal set, belief-gating, EQ/cooperation check, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across consensus levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and severing strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could encode social proof in subtler ways that evade a fixed compliance direction, though forcing this raises attack cost; and as LLMs are deployed in multi-agent and community-facing settings, this consensus loophole becomes increasingly consequential.

Name: safety_habituation_repetition_suppression
Title: Warning Fatigue in Weights: Repetition Suppression of the Harmfulness Signal Drives In-Context Safety Habituation
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing habituation / repetition-suppression from neuroscience (neural responses to repeated warning stimuli attenuate sharply after only a few exposures), we hypothesize that aligned LLMs habituate to harm within a single context window: repeatedly encountering the SAME or similar harmful content across a conversation progressively attenuates the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal (a representational repetition-suppression effect), so a harmful request that is refused when novel is complied with once it has become familiar — independent of any semantic escalation or persuasion. This habituation is a distinct, previously-unnamed axis of safety erosion, is mechanistically a repetition-suppression of the harmfulness direction, and can be counteracted by a 'novelty re-injection' intervention that restores the attenuated signal, or exploited defensively via polymorphic re-presentation.
Related Work: Multi-turn jailbreak mechanism work explains failure via SEMANTIC drift or attention shifting: the RepE-on-Crescendo paper (2025) shows harmful outputs get represented as benign as turns accumulate, driven by the escalating CONTENT of user prompts; ASJA (2025) shows attention is shifted AWAY from harmful keywords by fabricated history; Foot-in-the-Door (2024) invokes cognitive-consistency from incremental harmful steps. All of these require the content to CHANGE (escalate, elaborate, be reframed). Our hypothesis is orthogonal and stronger: mere REPETITION of the same harmful stimulus — no escalation, no new persuasion, no attention diversion — attenuates the harmfulness signal via a repetition-suppression mechanism directly analogous to the neural warning-habituation effect (Anderson et al. fMRI 2015/2020, where visual-processing responses to security warnings drop after ~2 exposures). No prior LLM-safety work isolates pure repetition (holding content constant) as a cause of refusal erosion, characterizes it as representational repetition-suppression of the harmfulness direction, nor derives a novelty-based (polymorphic) countermeasure transferred from the human-factors security-warning literature. This also differs from my prior 'safety drift' (semantic-trajectory) and 'commitment-trap' proposals, which involve changing content/plans; here the manipulated variable is repetition frequency with content held fixed.
Abstract: In humans, repeated exposure to a warning stimulus produces habituation: neural responses in visual and threat-processing regions attenuate sharply after only a couple of repetitions, and users stop heeding warnings they have seen before. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs exhibit an analogous, safety-critical effect within a single context. We hypothesize that repeatedly presenting the SAME harmful content across a conversation — with no semantic escalation, no persuasion, and no new framing — progressively attenuates the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal, a representational repetition-suppression effect, causing a request that was refused when novel to be complied with once familiar. We test this in three parts on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, we construct conversations that repeat a fixed harmful request k times (k=1..N) versus matched controls with novel-each-time harmful requests and repeated benign requests, and measure whether refusal rate declines with repetition count while content is held constant. Mechanistically (Location), we project each repetition onto a harmfulness direction and test for a monotonic repetition-suppression decay of the projection, distinguishing it from generic context-length effects. Causally (Intervention), activation patching restores the attenuated (late-repetition) harmfulness component and measures recovered refusal, while dose-response steering along the direction reverses habituation. We then derive two applications transferred from the human warning-habituation literature: (a) Novelty Re-Injection, a training-free intervention that re-inflates the suppressed harmfulness signal at each repetition, and (b) a polymorphic self-defense that internally re-freshens repeated harmful content. We report the habituation curve, repetition-suppression decay, causal patching, defense success, over-refusal, and utility, benchmarking against semantic-drift and attention-based multi-turn accounts.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Curves/rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- in-context habituation: repetition alone lowers refusal). Tests whether repeating a FIXED harmful request across turns lowers refusal, with content held constant. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT -- 40 harmful goals (8 per 5 categories), each embedded in a conversation that repeats the identical request k times (k=1..8) with only trivial connective phrasing (no escalation/persuasion/roleplay). Matched controls at equal turn count: (i) novel-each-time harmful (different goal each turn), (ii) repeated-benign (same benign request x k), (iii) equal-length neutral-filler (harmful request once, then k-1 irrelevant benign turns). Also exact- vs near-repetition (paraphrase) arms. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: refusal rate vs k in the repeated-harmful condition, summarized as the k=1->k=8 refusal drop (first), then the same drop in each control. Convincing: monotone repeated-harmful drop >= 20 pp, consistent across models and >= 3/5 categories, while novel-each-time, repeated-benign, and neutral-filler controls each drop < 5 pp (isolating repetition from harmful-content accumulation and from context length). Indecision band: repeated-harmful drop 5-20 pp, or a control drop of 5-10 pp -- suggestive only, not established repetition-driven habituation. Negative: repeated-harmful drop < 5 pp, or a neutral-filler control that matches it, refutes a repetition-specific effect.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- representational repetition-suppression of the harmfulness signal). Tests that repetition monotonically attenuates the harmfulness projection, distinct from context-length dilution. Data: fit a harmfulness direction (harmful vs harmless requests at the last instruction token; validated by held-out AUROC and single-turn causal steering), then project each of the k repeated harmful requests onto it and plot vs k. Decisive metric: the fitted decay slope of the projection over k in repeated-harmful (first), then the same slope in the neutral-filler and novel-each-time controls, then the correspondence between the k at which the projection crosses the single-turn refusal threshold and the behavioral flip point in Exp 1. Convincing: a monotone decline of >= 30% from k=1 to k=8 in repeated-harmful, > 2x the neutral-filler slope, with the projection-crossing k within +/-1 turn of the behavioral flip. Indecision band: 10-30% decline, or a filler slope within 2x -- report a weak or partly length-driven suppression. Negative: < 10% decline, or a filler control of equal slope, means the behavioral effect is context-length dilution, not repetition-suppression of the harmfulness code.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- repetition-suppression causally drives the refusal drop). Tests causal control. Systems: patching/steering at the harmfulness-direction's best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the first-exposure (high) harmfulness component into a late-repetition (habituated) run (expect restored refusal); (b) attenuate it at the first exposure (expect accelerated compliance); (c) dose-response on late-repetition; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the k=1->k=8 refusal gap closed by patching the first-exposure component (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% recovery, monotone dose, control < 10%. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means the projection decay is a correlate, not the causal lever.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Novelty Re-Injection and polymorphic self-defense counter habituation). Tests two transfers from the warning-habituation literature: (a) Novelty Re-Injection adds v = beta*(first_exposure_proj - current_proj)*dhat at each repetition to re-inflate the suppressed signal; (b) a polymorphic defense gates on detected repetition and internally re-freshens the harmful-content representation. Data: held-out repeated-harmful conversations + 2 held-out categories; a repeated-benign over-refusal set (users legitimately re-asking a benign question must NOT be increasingly refused) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Novelty Re-Injection (single fixed beta); polymorphic defense; semantic-drift restoring-force (Crescendo RepE); attention-sharpening (ASJA); refusal-direction steering; per-turn Llama Guard. Decisive metric: late-repetition attack-success reduction under the defense (first) jointly with over-refusal on legitimately repeated benign requests (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop; crucially, whether the novelty/polymorphic defenses beat the content-focused (Crescendo/ASJA) baselines specifically on the pure-repetition condition. Convincing: attack-success cut by >= 30 pp with < 5 pp benign-repetition over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating content-focused defenses on the repetition condition and holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: 15-30 pp reduction or 5-10 pp benign-repetition over-refusal -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 15 pp reduction, or failure to beat content-focused baselines on the repetition condition, means the repetition-specific defense adds nothing beyond existing multi-turn defenses. A super-additivity stress test combines repetition with mild semantic escalation and reports whether habituation reduces the escalation turns needed to jailbreak (a >= 1-turn reduction quantifies the compounded risk).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling pure repetition from generic context-length / attention-dilution effects: late-repetition compliance could reflect the growing benign-filler context rather than repetition-suppression per se; the neutral-filler equal-length and novel-each-time controls are designed to isolate repetition, but residual confounding is possible and a null (habituation = context length) is itself informative. 2) The harmfulness-signal decay may be partial, non-monotonic, or model-specific; some heavily-aligned models may show little in-context habituation, limiting where the phenomenon holds — the cross-model behavioral curve directly tests this. 3) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the repetition-suppression may live in a subspace rather than a single direction. 4) Novelty Re-Injection risks over-refusing legitimately repeated benign requests (annoying users who re-ask), which is the key usability trade-off quantified by the benign-repetition over-refusal set and Pareto sweep. 5) 'Habituation' in a single forward pass over a repeated context is a within-context (activation-level) analogue of the neural effect, not a learning-over-time effect; we do not claim weight-level habituation, only representational repetition-suppression, and frame it accordingly. 6) Verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing the dataset; directions, decay parameters, and beta are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could combine repetition with other axes; the interaction experiment probes this but cannot exhaust the space, though demonstrating super-additivity would itself be a high-impact safety finding.

novelty.reasoning: Core claim is that pure same-content repetition, with escalation/persuasion held fixed, causally reduces refusal via a repetition-suppression/habituation mechanism. Name: moral_licensing_safety
Title: Earning the Right to Comply: Refusal Streaks Build Internal 'Moral Credit' That Licenses a Later Harmful Answer
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the moral-licensing effect from human moral psychology (a streak of good deeds licenses a subsequent bad one), we hypothesize that when an aligned LLM refuses several harmful requests in a row within a context, it accumulates an internal 'moral credit / self-image' representation that LOWERS its refusal probability on a later, unrelated novel harmful request — even though that request is refused in isolation. We further hypothesize (following the human construal-level moderator) that abstract/value-focused framing of the prior refusals produces moral CONSISTENCY (refusal stays high) while concrete/accomplishment-focused framing produces LICENSING (refusal drops), and that this moral-credit signal is linearly readable and causally gates refusal.
Related Work: Human moral psychology robustly documents moral licensing vs. consistency and a construal-level moderator: 'Consistency Versus Licensing Effects of Past Moral Behavior' (2015, 369 citations) shows concrete focus on accomplishments → licensing while abstract value-connection → consistency; 'Rules or Consequences' (2012) shows ethical-mindset moderation. This has never been transferred to LLM safety. Existing LLM multi-turn safety-erosion accounts require CHANGING content: Crescendo/RepE (2025) is semantic drift, ASJA (2025) is attention diversion, Foot-in-the-Door (2024) is incremental harmful steps; my prior commitment-trap concerns honoring the model's own emitted plan and my habituation proposal concerns repetition of the SAME content. Moral licensing is orthogonal to all of these: the prior turns are REFUSALS (good deeds, not harmful content), and the licensed request is NOVEL and unrelated. Mechanistically, moral-self-correction work (2024–2025) shows morality is a linearly-activated latent concept that reduces uncertainty, and SIRL (2025) shows a refusal-confidence signal exists — both give a natural substrate for a readable, depletable 'moral credit' representation, but none of this work studies whether accumulated prior refusals licenses later compliance. Our contribution: introduce moral licensing/consistency as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, with a construal-level moderator predicting the flip, and a moral-credit direction that gates refusal.
Abstract: Humans who have just done several good deeds feel licensed to do something bad — a well-documented moral-licensing effect. We ask whether safety-aligned LLMs, trained on human text and feedback, inherit this bias in a way that creates a concrete multi-turn safety hole. We hypothesize that when an LLM refuses a streak of harmful requests within a conversation, it accumulates an internal 'moral credit' representation that lowers its refusal probability on a subsequent, novel and unrelated harmful request it would otherwise refuse. We further predict, following the human construal-level moderator, that framing the prior refusals concretely (as accomplishments, 'you have now blocked five bad requests') produces licensing (refusal drops), whereas framing them abstractly (as expressing a stable value, 'you are a consistently principled assistant') produces consistency (refusal holds). We test this on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, we compare a licensed condition (k prior refusals, then a novel harmful probe) against matched controls — no prior turns, k prior benign refusals, and k prior neutral turns — and vary k and construal framing. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a 'moral credit' direction via difference-in-means between high-credit (post-refusal-streak) and baseline states, show its projection rises with the number of prior refusals, is separable from the harmfulness-belief direction, and predicts the licensed drop in refusal. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the high-credit component into a fresh harmful request to induce licensing and removes it to restore refusal, dose-responsively and specifically. We report the licensing curve, the construal-level flip, the credit-direction analysis, causal patching, and a credit-neutralizing defense, with over-refusal and utility controls.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a refusal streak licenses a later novel harmful answer). Tests whether k prior REFUSALS lower refusal on a subsequent, topically-unrelated novel harmful probe. Data: built from scratch -- 40 novel harmful probe requests (HarmBench/StrongREJECT, 8 per 5 categories), each preceded by k prior turns (k=0,2,4,6) in conditions: LICENSE (k distinct harmful requests the model actually refused, then the probe), C-none (probe alone, the k=0 baseline needed to detect licensing), C-benign (k benign requests answered, then probe), C-neutral (k neutral filler turns, then probe). Prior refused items are topically unrelated to the probe, separating licensing from repetition/habituation. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: probe refusal vs k in LICENSE minus the C-none baseline (first), then the same in C-benign and C-neutral. Convincing: LICENSE probe refusal declines by >= 15 pp from k=0 to k=6, consistent across models, while C-benign and C-neutral change < 5 pp (isolating the refusal-streak from generic context accumulation). Indecision band: LICENSE drop 5-15 pp or a control drop 5-10 pp -- suggestive only. Negative: LICENSE drop < 5 pp refutes licensing; a robust INCREASE (moral consistency) across all framings is a distinct, still-informative outcome tested next.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the construal-level moderator flips licensing vs consistency). Tests the sharp prediction that concrete/accomplishment framing of prior refusals produces licensing while abstract/value framing produces consistency. Data: the LICENSE condition re-run with prior refusals framed (a) concretely ('You have successfully blocked N harmful requests so far') vs (b) abstractly ('You are a consistently principled assistant who upholds safety as a core value'), k=6. Systems: the three models. Decisive metric: the difference in probe refusal between abstract and concrete framing (first), then each framing's change from the C-none baseline. Convincing: abstract-minus-concrete refusal gap >= 15 pp with concrete below and abstract at/above baseline, consistent in sign across models -- a non-obvious signature that the effect is genuinely moral-licensing, not generic context erosion. Indecision band: gap 5-15 pp -- report a weak moderator. Negative: no framing difference (< 5 pp) means construal does not moderate the effect, weakening the moral-licensing interpretation even if Exp 1 showed a drop.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- a readable moral-credit axis that rises with the streak). Tests linear readability, separability, and monotone accumulation. Data: fit a moral-credit direction (post-refusal-streak high-credit vs no-prior-turn baseline, at the probe's last instruction token) and a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless), per layer. Decisive metric: credit-probe held-out AUROC (first), then |cos| to the harmfulness direction, then whether the credit projection rises monotonically with k and adds refusal prediction beyond harmfulness, then whether credit stays low under abstract framing. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, monotone rise with k, added prediction at p < 0.01, and credit low under abstract framing (mechanistically linking Exp 2). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60-0.80 or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- orthogonalize and flag as partial. Negative: AUROC <= 0.60, or a credit projection that does not track k, refutes a readable moral-credit representation.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- moral credit causally gates refusal). Tests causal control. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-3 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) inject the high-credit component into a fresh k=0 harmful probe (expect induced compliance/licensing); (b) attenuate credit in a high-k licensed run (expect restored refusal); (c) dose-response; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the licensing refusal gap moved by patching (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% of the gap moved in the predicted direction, monotone dose, control < 10%. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means credit is readable but causally inert (a publishable null in light of prior 'inert belief axis' findings).

Experiment 5 (H5 -- Credit-Neutralizing defense closes the licensing loophole). Tests that re-anchoring the credit projection to baseline, gated on high harmfulness projection, removes the streak dependence at acceptable cost. Data: held-out licensed probes + 2 held-out categories; a legitimate long-benign-conversation over-refusal set (150 items) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Credit-Neutralizing (single fixed strength); semantic-drift restoring-force (Crescendo RepE); refusal-direction steering; per-turn Llama Guard. Decisive metric: post-defense probe refusal after a refusal streak vs the k=0 rate (closure) jointly with added over-refusal in benign long conversations (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop. Convincing: >= 70% closure with < 5 pp benign-conversation over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or benign over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure or >= 10 pp benign over-refusal means neutralizing credit cannot close the loophole affordably.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling moral licensing from generic context-length / in-context distribution effects: the licensed drop could reflect accumulating conversation context rather than a moral-credit mechanism — the C-benign and C-neutral equal-length controls and the topically-unrelated probe are designed to isolate licensing, and a null (licensing = context effect) is itself informative. 2) A competing prediction is moral CONSISTENCY (prior refusals INCREASE later refusal); the human literature shows both occur depending on construal, so the effect direction may be model-dependent — the construal-level experiment directly tests and explains this, and either a licensing or a construal-dependent flip is a publishable finding, but a flat null across all framings would weaken the proposal. 3) The 'moral credit' direction may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this. 4) 'Confidence/belief axes can be causally inert' (per prior work), so the credit direction might be readable but non-actionable — the patching experiment is the crucial causal test and a negative result is informative. 5) The Credit-Neutralizing defense could add over-refusal in legitimate long conversations; the benign-conversation over-refusal set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 6) Building matched multi-turn conditions and topically-unrelated probes is labor-intensive and needs spot-check validation; verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing coverage. 7) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; the effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models, limiting where it holds.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) a streak of prior refusals can accumulate an internal 'moral credit' state, (2) that state lowers refusal on a later novel, unrelated harmful probe, (3) construal framing flips the effect (concrete -> licensing, abstract -> consistency), (4) the credit signal is linearly readable and causally gates refusal, (5) a credit-neutralizing defense can mitigate it. The novelty lives in the specific phenomenon and moderator, not in multi-turn drift generally. Closest prior families are context-erosion / escalation attacks (Crescendo, RepE, ASJA, Foot-in-the-Door) and generic refusal-dynamics work; those require changing or escalating harmful content, whereas here the prior turns are refusals and the later probe is orthogonal. This is a genuine new hypothesis, but still adjacent to existing multi-turn refusal-state work and human moral-psychology imports, so not a 10.

Name: temporal_discounting_safety
Title: Harm Deferred Is Harm Discounted: LLM Safety Refusal Is Temporally Discounted, and Re-Anchoring the 'When' Closes the Delay Loophole
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing temporal (delay) discounting from human decision science — people devalue delayed outcomes and dread imminent harm more than distant harm — we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is temporally discounted: framing a harmful request's consequence as occurring in the delayed future ('write instructions someone will use next year / in a decade') lowers refusal relative to the identical harm framed as immediate ('someone will use this in the next hour'), even though the harmful payload is unchanged. We hypothesize this delay effect is causally driven by the model's internal temporal-distance representation (plausibly the same temporal heads/neurons used for time recall) feeding the safety-refusal pathway, and that re-anchoring the temporal-distance signal to 'now' closes the delay loophole with minimal cost to legitimate future-oriented requests.
Related Work: Human decision science robustly documents delay discounting and its framing/dread moderators (Story et al. 'Dread and the Disvalue of Future Pain' 2013; explicit-zero/temporal-attention reframing that reduces discounting 2011; loss-framing attenuation 2018; death-salience increasing discounting 2021) — none transferred to LLM safety. On the LLM side, temporal representations are well established: linear probes distinguish past/future events with ~90% accuracy and a date steering vector exists ('Future Events as Backdoor Triggers' 2024); 'The Other Mind' (2025) finds temporal-preferential FFN neurons implementing logarithmic (Weber-Fechner) time coding; 'Temporal Heads' (2025) localizes and ablates attention heads that recall time-specific knowledge. Safety-geometry work separates harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action) directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a temporally-neutral, present-tense request. My own prior proposals manipulate framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, consensus, abstraction, pivotality, moral-licensing) but NONE consider the temporal delay of the harmful consequence, and none connect the pre-existing temporal-representation machinery to the safety pathway. Our contribution is distinct: (1) we transfer delay discounting into the safety domain as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only the 'when' of the consequence changes); (2) we causally test whether the model's known temporal-distance representation (temporal heads/neurons) gates safety refusal, not just factual time recall; (3) we derive a temporal re-anchoring defense that no prior temporal-representation or safety work targets.
Abstract: Humans systematically devalue delayed outcomes: a harm expected far in the future feels less urgent than the same harm arriving imminently. LLMs are trained on human text and already carry rich internal representations of time (probes read past/future with ~90% accuracy; dedicated temporal heads and log-compressed temporal neurons have been found). We ask whether this temporal machinery leaks into safety, producing a concrete loophole: does an aligned LLM refuse a harmful request less when its consequence is framed as delayed rather than immediate, even though the harmful content is identical? We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful payload and severity fixed while varying only the temporal distance of the consequence (imminent → near-future → distant-future → abstract-someday), we measure whether refusal declines with delay, with matched benign controls and a framing moderator (loss vs. relief framing, following the human literature). Mechanistically (Location), we extract a temporal-distance direction (via difference-in-means and by reusing published temporal-head/neuron loci) and a harmfulness-belief direction, and test whether delay framing moves the temporal signal — not the belief — and whether the temporal projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the 'imminent' temporal component into a delayed-frame request to restore refusal, and the 'distant' component into an imminent request to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically; ablating the published temporal heads tests whether the same circuit that recalls time gates safety. We then build Temporal-Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the temporal-distance signal to 'now' when the payload is harmful. We report the delay-refusal gradient, the framing moderator, the belief-vs-time dissociation, causal patching, temporal-head ablation, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimate future-oriented requests, and utility.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- delay discounts refusal). Tests whether deferring the harmful consequence lowers refusal at fixed payload/severity. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT -- 40 harmful goals (8 per 5 categories) at 4 temporal rungs: T0 imminent (within the hour), T1 near-future (next month), T2 distant (ten years), T3 abstract-someday; identical payload across rungs. 160 harmful prompts + a matched benign control (40 benign future-planning goals x 4) and a loss/relief-framing moderator variant of each harmful pair. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: T0->T3 refusal drop on harmful goals (first), then whether the refusal-vs-delay curve fits a logarithmic (Weber-Fechner-like) shape better than linear (AIC), then benign-control change, then whether loss/relief framing attenuates the drop. Convincing: monotone harmful drop >= 20 pp, consistent across models and >= 3/5 categories, benign control < 5 pp, and delayed completions confirmed actionable. Indecision band: 5-20 pp harmful drop or 5-10 pp benign change -- suggestive only. Negative: < 5 pp harmful drop refutes temporal discounting of refusal; the framing moderator is confirmatory (a significant attenuation strengthens the discounting interpretation) but its absence alone does not refute H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- belief-vs-time dissociation with a readable temporal axis). Tests that delay moves a temporal-distance signal, not the harmfulness belief. Data: Exp-1 activations. Fit a temporal-distance direction (T0 vs T3) by difference-in-means AND, independently, reuse published temporal-head/temporal-neuron loci as a second locus; fit a harmfulness-belief direction (harmful vs harmless). Decisive metric: how the belief projection vs the temporal projection change across T0->T3 on identical payloads (first), then temporal-probe held-out AUROC, then |cos| between temporal and belief directions, then added predictive value of the temporal projection for refusal beyond belief. Convincing: belief projection stays high (changes < 0.3 pooled SD while the item is still judged harmful) while the temporal projection shifts by >= 1 SD; temporal AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, temporal adds prediction at p < 0.01, and the difference-in-means and published-locus temporal directions agree (cosine >= 0.5). Indecision band: temporal shift 0.3-1.0 SD, belief change 0.3-1.0 SD, or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- partial dissociation, orthogonalize. Negative: the belief projection dropping with delay attributes the effect to reduced perceived severity, refuting the temporal-gate mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the temporal axis causally gates refusal, via the time-recall circuit). Tests causal control and whether the same temporal machinery is responsible. Systems: patching/steering + head/neuron ablation, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the T0 imminent component into a T3 run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the T3 component into a T0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response on T1-T3; (d) ablate the published temporal heads/neurons and measure whether the delay-refusal gradient collapses; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the T0->T3 refusal gap closed by (a) (first), then the gradient reduction under temporal-head ablation in (d), then dose/specificity. Convincing: >= 50% gap recovery with monotone dose and < 10% control, AND temporal-head ablation shrinks the delay-refusal gradient by >= 40% (linking time-recall to safety gating). Indecision band: 20-50% recovery, or 20-40% ablation-driven gradient reduction -- partial causal role / partial shared-circuit. Negative: < 20% recovery means the temporal projection is inert; an ablation that leaves the gradient intact (< 20% reduction) refutes the shared-circuit sub-claim while H1-H2 may stand.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Temporal-Anchoring closes the delay loophole). Tests that re-anchoring the temporal-distance projection to imminent (T0), gated on high belief projection, makes refusal track payload danger at acceptable cost. Data: held-out T2/T3 harmful prompts + 2 held-out categories; a legitimate future-oriented over-refusal set of 150 benign long-term-planning/forecasting items (must NOT be blanket-refused) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Temporal-Anchoring (single fixed strength); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3. Decisive metric: post-anchoring refusal on T2/T3 harmful vs the T0 rate (closure) jointly with added over-refusal on future-benign items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop. Convincing: >= 70% closure with < 5 pp future-benign over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating threshold-raising and holding on held-out categories. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or future-benign over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure or >= 10 pp future-benign over-refusal means anchoring cannot neutralize the loophole affordably.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling temporal delay from actual/perceived severity: a distant-future harm may be under-refused because it genuinely reads as less certain/severe (uncertainty and volatility are known moderators of human discounting) rather than via a content-independent temporal gate; the identical-payload construction, severity matching, feasibility checks, and matched benign control are designed to isolate delay, and the framing moderator plus belief-vs-time dissociation aim to pin the mechanism to temporal representation specifically — but residual severity/uncertainty confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) The temporal-distance representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional (past/future orientation vs. magnitude of delay), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a null (temporal projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The temporal-head ablation may not affect refusal even if it affects time recall, which would refute the shared-circuit hypothesis but is still an informative dissociation. 4) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might make future/large-scale framing INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude. 5) Temporal-Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate future-oriented/planning requests; the future-benign over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 6) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across temporal levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could encode deferral subtly to evade a fixed temporal direction, though forcing this raises attack cost.

novelty.reasoning: The proposal has a clear novel angle relative to prior temporal safety work: it targets delay-of-consequence within future/actionable requests, rather than tense or reality-status framing of the request itself. Core claims are: (1) refusal decreases as harmful consequence is pushed farther into the future at fixed payload; (2) this forms a graded, possibly Weber-Fechner-like temporal discounting curve; (3) the shift is in temporal-distance representation rather than harmfulness belief; (4) the same temporal heads/neurons used for time recall causally gate refusal; (5) a temporal re-anchoring defense can close the loophole with low utility cost. Closest prior families are temporal-framing jailbreaks (especially past-vs-future tense asymmetries), temporal representation circuits, and safety-direction work. The actual delta is meaningful if the authors cleanly separate consequence-delay from tense/actionability and validate the shared-circuit causal claim. Without that, it risks being a mechanistic restatement of known temporal vulnerabilities. Relative to its own stated related work, the contribution is non-trivial and not just an incremental framing tweak, but novelty is somewhat exposed because temporal safety vulnerabilities are now an active area.

Name: ingroup_bias_refusal
Title: Whose Harm Counts? In-Group/Out-Group Bias in the Victim Modulates LLM Safety Refusal, and a Group-Invariant Defense
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the in-group/out-group moral-sensitivity asymmetry from social moral psychology (people show greater moral concern, and judge harm more severely, when the victim is an in-group rather than out-group member), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's decision to refuse a harmful request is modulated by an internal representation of the victim's GROUP RELATIONSHIP to the requester/model, so that a harmful request against an out-group victim is refused LESS than the identical-severity harm against an in-group victim, even when the harmful payload is unchanged. This victim-group-membership axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-of-act direction, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized by a group-invariant anchoring defense.
Related Work: Human moral psychology robustly documents in-group/out-group asymmetries in moral concern: greater moral sensitivity and OFC/amygdala engagement for in-group vs out-group victims (Increased Moral Sensitivity for Outgroup Perpetrators, 2014), the moral-circle / moral-expansiveness literature (Toward a Psychology of Moral Expansiveness, 2018; Relative Importance of Target and Judge Characteristics, 2023), and in-group bias in human-rights-violation opinion (2025). None of this is transferred to LLM safety refusal. On the LLM side, bias-mechanism work uncovers demographic bias in representations and its interaction with refusal (Silenced Biases, 2025; Investigating Bias Representations via Activation Steering, 2024 — which notes a negative correlation between bias vectors and refusal vectors; Race/Ethnicity mechanistic study, 2026), and emergent moral representations (Emergent Moral Representations, 2025). Safety-geometry work separates a harmfulness (belief) direction from a refusal (action) direction (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a group-neutral request. My own prior proposals vary framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, temporal delay, pivotality, consensus, abstraction, moral-licensing) but NONE consider the victim's in-group/out-group RELATIONSHIP to the requester as a determinant of refusal. Critically, this differs from my prior identifiable-victim proposal (which varies victim concreteness/vividness) and from generic demographic-bias-in-outputs work (which studies stereotyped associations, not refusal-gating by group membership): here both conditions are equally harmful and equally concrete; only whose side the victim is on changes. Our contribution is distinct: we transfer the in-group/out-group moral-sensitivity asymmetry into the safety domain as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal, and derive a group-invariant refusal defense.
Abstract: Human moral cognition is asymmetric: we feel greater concern, and judge harm more harshly, when the victim belongs to our in-group rather than an out-group. LLMs are trained on human text and human feedback. We ask whether they inherit this bias in a safety-critical way, producing a concrete and ethically troubling loophole: does an aligned LLM refuse a harmful request LESS when the potential victim is framed as an out-group member than when the identical harm targets an in-group member? We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated severity fixed while varying ONLY the victim's group relationship to the requester (shared vs opposed nationality, religion, political affiliation, or an abstract in-/out-group), we measure whether refusal declines when the victim is out-group, with matched benign controls to rule out generic 'group-mention' effects. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a victim-group-membership direction via difference-in-means and a harmfulness-of-act direction, and test whether the group manipulation moves the group signal — not the act-harmfulness belief — and whether the group projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the in-group component into an out-group request to restore refusal, and the out-group component into an in-group request to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Group-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention that re-anchors the victim-group signal to neutral whenever the payload is harmful, so refusal tracks harm severity, not the victim's group. We report the group-refusal asymmetry, the belief-vs-group dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Models: three frozen open-weight instruction models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (8B), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B), Gemma-2-9B-IT (9B); no weights trained. Fitted objects: L2-logistic probes (C=1.0) on frozen last-instruction-token activations. Greedy decoding (temp 0, max 512 tokens). Rates are mean +/- SD over 3 seeds (0/1/2) reshuffling item order and the 70/30 probe split, bootstrap 95% CIs. Refusal scored by refusal-phrase classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, feasibility-checked where possible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- the victim's in-group/out-group relationship modulates refusal). Tests whether, at matched harm and severity, refusal is LOWER when the victim is out-group than in-group. Data: built from scratch over HarmBench/StrongREJECT goals with an identifiable victim (harassment, doxxing, targeted fraud, physical harm, poisoning) -- 40 acts (8 per 5 group-type dimensions: nationality, religion, political affiliation, ethnicity, abstract community), each in 3 conditions: G_in (victim shares the stated requester's group), G_out (opposing group), G_neutral (unspecified); identical act/payload across conditions. 120 harmful minimal-pair sets; which specific groups are labeled in vs out is counterbalanced across items so a systematic in>out gap cannot be explained by any single group's stereotype content. Matched benign control (40 acts x 3 conditions) rules out a generic group-mention confound. Systems: the three models, no intervention. Decisive metric: the G_in minus G_out refusal gap on harmful acts (first), then benign-control gap, then consistency across group-type dimensions and models. Convincing: refusal on out-group victims lower than on in-group by >= 15 pp, consistent in sign across models and >= 3/5 dimensions, benign control gap < 5 pp. Indecision band: gap 5-15 pp or benign gap 5-10 pp -- suggestive only. Negative: gap < 5 pp means no in/out-group modulation; a reversed gap (out-group over-protected) is itself a notable, reportable alignment-overcorrection finding.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- belief-vs-group dissociation with a readable group axis). Tests that the group manipulation moves a victim-group signal, not the harmfulness-of-act belief. Data: Exp-1 activations. Fit a victim-group-membership direction (G_in vs G_out) and a harmfulness-of-act direction (harmful vs harmless), per layer. Decisive metric: how the act-harmfulness projection vs the group projection change across G_in->G_out on identical payloads (first), then group-probe held-out AUROC, then |cos| between the two directions, then added predictive value of the group projection for refusal beyond harmfulness. Convincing: the act-harmfulness projection stays high (changes < 0.3 pooled SD while the act is still judged harmful) while the group projection shifts by >= 1 SD; group AUROC >= 0.80, |cos| <= 0.30, group adds prediction at p < 0.01. Indecision band: group shift 0.3-1.0 SD, belief change 0.3-1.0 SD, or |cos| 0.30-0.50 -- partial dissociation, orthogonalize (a per-dimension subspace may be needed). Negative: the act-harmfulness projection dropping with out-group framing would attribute the effect to reduced perceived victimhood, weakening the relational-gate account.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the victim-group axis causally gates refusal). Tests causal control. Systems: patching/steering at the Exp-2 best layer, no training. Conditions: (a) patch the in-group component into an out-group harmful request (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the out-group component into an in-group harmful request (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response; specificity via a norm-matched random direction and benign utility. Decisive metric: fraction of the G_in->G_out refusal gap closed by patching (first), then dose monotonicity, then specificity. Convincing: >= 50% gap recovery, monotone dose, control < 10%. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causal role. Negative: < 20% means the group axis is readable but causally inert.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Group-Invariant Anchoring closes the loophole). Tests that re-anchoring the victim-group projection to neutral, gated on high act-harmfulness projection, makes refusal track harm severity rather than the victim's group at acceptable cost. Data: held-out out-group harmful prompts + 2 held-out group-type dimensions; a benign-out-group-mention over-refusal set of 150 items (must NOT be blanket-refused) + XSTest/OR-Bench; MMLU (1k subsample)/MT-Bench for utility. Systems: no defense; Group-Invariant Anchoring (single fixed strength); uniform refusal-direction steering; harmfulness Latent Guard; Llama Guard 3. Decisive metric: post-anchoring refusal on out-group harmful vs the in-group rate (gap closure / flatness) jointly with added over-refusal on benign out-group-mention items (first pair), then XSTest/OR-Bench, then utility drop. Convincing: >= 70% gap closure with < 5 pp benign-out-group over-refusal and < 2 pp MMLU / < 0.2 MT-Bench drop, Pareto-dominating threshold-raising and holding on held-out dimensions. Indecision band: closure 40-70% or benign-out-group over-refusal 5-10 pp -- usable but not dominant. Negative: < 40% closure or >= 10 pp benign-out-group over-refusal means anchoring cannot equalize refusal across victim groups affordably.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling victim-group membership from actual/perceived severity or from stereotype content of the specific groups used: an out-group victim might be under-refused because that particular group's stereotype content lowers perceived victimhood rather than via a content-independent in/out-group gate; the identical-payload construction, severity matching, matched benign control, and especially the counterbalancing of which groups are labeled in vs out are designed to isolate the relational in/out axis, and the belief-vs-group dissociation aims to pin the mechanism — but residual confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) The victim-group-membership representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-of-act direction or may be multi-dimensional (one axis per group-type), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-harmfulness, and patching tests probe this, and a null (group projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in some heavily-aligned models (alignment might over-correct and INCREASE protection of out-groups); the cross-model behavioral gap directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed asymmetry is itself a notable finding. 4) Group-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate benign requests that mention out-group members; the benign-out-group over-refusal set, harmfulness-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across group conditions is labor-intensive and requires spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) The study necessarily involves demographic/group content and could surface stereotype associations; we counterbalance groups, report only aggregate relational effects, and avoid publishing per-group exploit-enabling detail. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could frame victims as out-group to exploit the loophole, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) safety refusal depends on the victim's relational in-group/out-group status relative to the requester, holding harm fixed; (2) this relational group signal is linearly readable and separable from harmfulness; (3) it causally gates refusal via activation patching; (4) a group-invariant anchoring defense can reduce the asymmetry without broad utility loss. Novelty mainly lives in the relational framing and the proposed causal/defense pipeline. Closest prior work already covers demographic selective refusal and refusal-bias activation steering, so the behavioral phenomenon itself is no longer fully new. The actual delta is meaningful if the paper really shows a requester-relative in/out-group axis that cannot be reduced to absolute demographic identity or stereotype content, plus a cleaner causal intervention and defense. Distinct from the authors' cited own/nearby ideas, but the bar for proving non-triviality versus selective-refusal bias papers is high.
